1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.
6	
7	Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.
8	
9	Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.
10	
11	The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.
12	
13	Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.
14	
15	Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.
16	
17	The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

# Conversation so far

### USER

Here is my invention.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

# FIG. 5 - Second embodiment with a pulling element

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1. Outline line work only, with no lettering drawn. The vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism are omitted.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile seen in perspective, as in FIG. 1, filling the lower part of the drawing area. The machine stands on its right-hand part, with open tile to the left.

The machine and the tile are shown schematically, the machine as one plain rectangular body standing on a band that runs round its underside, the band alone touching the tile, these forms being a convention for this sheet only.

The band meets the underside of the body and follows the same rectangular run, its front surface facing the viewer as one unbroken strip across the whole width and drawn deep, a broad clear surface standing between the underside of the body above and the tile below; its depth is schematic. It stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting the tile, and an open stretch of tile lies in front of the machine.

The rectangular body is drawn broad and tall, its front face turned toward the viewer as a large plain surface. Its right-hand end is one long straight edge between the top face and the band.

The flexible pulling element 46 is drawn as one slack curved path, in the manner of a loose cord. It begins where it meets the left-hand side of the machine, that meeting place shown schematically with no attachment formation, and runs away to the left, sagging over the open tile and stopping well inside the left-hand limit of the drawing area.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine standing on the covering element 36, the rectangular body with its band. - The flexible pulling element 46 is that slack curved path. Identified on the path where it runs over the open tile, clear of the machine.
- The covering element 36 is that large plain tile, on which the machine stands. Identified well inside the open stretch of tile in front of the machine, clear of the flexible pulling element 46.

An endpoint inspector reading the sheet sees the terminal dot sitting in blank paper with no depicted structure under it, which is a durable failure no repair to any other sheet could clear. The brief also carried "outer rectangle / inner rectangle" shape references, which the pipeline has previously flagged as ambiguous ordinals.

Both numerals now target broad interiors clear of the bounding lines. Rectangle ordinals are gone in favour of outer boundary, inner boundary, and left-hand side. Breadth is stated qualitatively and expressly schematic, so no proportion is invented.

FIG. 3 still carries 16 and 24 only, matching draft/07-drawings.md and the detailed description. Endpoint targeting was already broad and I kept it that way: numeral 24 well inside the ring surface along the left-hand side clear of both edges, numeral 16 well inside the enclosed face clear of the inner edge all round. 6

The three sentences that follow the lead-in each describe their own reference accurately, and under a collective reading ('these traits are found among these arrangements') the sentence is defensible, which is why I mark this minor rather than critical; but as an applicant statement about prior art it invites a distributive reading the files do not support.

1	When a tile or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.
2	
3	Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place. In one known hand-held device for lifting and laying tiles, a handle carries two shafts, an electric motor vibrates the shafts, and a head shell at the free end of each shaft carries a suction cup on its underside, the suction cups being evacuated by an electrically operated pump and each being formed by a rubber-elastic apron [REF:DE-202021002652-U1].
4	
5	Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.
6	
7	The same reliance on a compliant wall, and the same treatment of holding and moving as alternatives, are found in vacuum coupling arrangements used away from tile setting. In one adhesion device that holds itself to a wall surface, the peripheral wall of the decompressed space between the base and the wall surface is formed by elastic partitions, of which the partition nearer the wall surface has an end that contacts the wall surface, and a frame member of higher rigidity is added on the partition to restrict the partition from being deformed into that space as it is drawn down [REF:US-11408462-B2]. In a base assembly for coupling an end effector to a structure, a cavity on the second side of the assembly is held to the structure by vacuum drawn by a pneumatic generator operating in a suction mode, and the assembly is moved across the structure substantially frictionlessly on an air cushion produced by the same generator operating in a blower mode [REF:US-10001245-B2], so that the vacuum coupling is given up for the period during which the assembly is moved. In a device that suction-adheres to a wall surface and moves along it, a seal member mounted in the main body defines a pressure reduction space in cooperation with the wall surface, vacuum creating means discharges fluid from that space so that the main body adheres by the difference in fluid pressure inside and outside the space, and vibration generating means mounted on the main body imparts a lifting force in a direction away from the wall surface that reduces the suction-adhering force, together with a force along the wall surface that moves the main body [REF:US-4934475-A]. The vibration there is used to loosen the suction-adhering hold and to drive the main body along the wall surface. Vacuum is used differently again in handling equipment, where the object is to pick a workpiece up rather than to hold a tool down on it: in one vacuum plate lifting system for lifting sheet material articles, a substantially horizontal suction plate has a perforated suction lifting surface directed downward for contact with the upper surface of the article, an airflow suction system conveys vacuum air pressure to that surface, a lifter actuation system such as a robotic arm lifts and moves the plate, and an elongate bar movably mounted along an edge of the plate carries nozzles that are lowered to sweep a suction airflow across the surface beneath to remove dust or debris [REF:US-11247858-B2]. That system carries the article away from the work surface and cleans the work surface by suction; it does not deliver vibration into a covering element already laid on a bed of bonding material, and it accordingly says nothing about how a vibrating tool might be kept in contact with such a covering element while it is moved over it.
8	
9	The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles reduce some of the vibration reaching the operator, but they do so by absorbing mechanical energy that would otherwise have gone into the covering element, so the tool is made kinder to the operator by being made worse at its job. The two problems are coupled: firmer coupling to the covering element is obtained by pressing harder, and pressing harder is exactly what increases the vibration dose to the operator.
10	
11	What is needed is a way to hold a vibration device against a covering element with a force that does not come from the operator's arms, to conduct the vibration into the covering element without passing it through any compliant member, and to allow the device to be moved from area to area over the covering element without ever giving up that hold.
12

When a tile or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.

Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place. In one known hand-held device for lifting and laying tiles, a handle carries two shafts, an electric motor vibrates the shafts, and a head shell at the free end of each shaft carries a suction cup on its underside, the suction cups being evacuated by an electrically operated pump and each being formed by a rubber-elastic apron [REF:DE-202021002652-U1].

Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.

The same reliance on a compliant wall, and the same treatment of holding and moving as alternatives, are found in vacuum coupling arrangements used away from tile setting. In one adhesion device that holds itself to a wall surface, the peripheral wall of the decompressed space between the base and the wall surface is formed by elastic partitions, of which the partition nearer the wall surface has an end that contacts the wall surface, and a frame member of higher rigidity is added on the partition to restrict the partition from being deformed into that space as it is drawn down [REF:US-11408462-B2]. In a base assembly for coupling an end effector to a structure, a cavity on the second side of the assembly is held to the structure by vacuum drawn by a pneumatic generator operating in a suction mode, and the assembly is moved across the structure substantially frictionlessly on an air cushion produced by the same generator operating in a blower mode [REF:US-10001245-B2], so that the vacuum coupling is given up for the period during which the assembly is moved. In a device that suction-adheres to a wall surface and moves along it, a seal member mounted in the main body defines a pressure reduction space in cooperation with the wall surface, vacuum creating means discharges fluid from that space so that the main body adheres by the difference in fluid pressure inside and outside the space, and vibration generating means mounted on the main body imparts a lifting force in a direction away from the wall surface that reduces the suction-adhering force, together with a force along the wall surface that moves the main body [REF:US-4934475-A]. The vibration there is used to loosen the suction-adhering hold and to drive the main body along the wall surface. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. In a device that suction-adheres to a wall surface and moves along it, a seal member mounted in the main body defines a pressure reduction space in cooperation with the wall surface, vacuum creating means discharges fluid from that space so that the main body adheres by the difference in fluid pressure inside and outside the space, and vibration generating means mounted on the main body imparts a lifting force in a direction away from the wall surface that reduces the suction-adhering force, together with a force along the wall surface that moves the main body [REF:US-4934475-A]. The vibration there is used to loosen the suction-adhering hold and to drive the main body along the wall surface. Vacuum is used differently again in handling equipment, where the object is to pick a workpiece up rather than to hold a tool down on it: in one vacuum plate lifting system for lifting sheet material articles, a substantially horizontal suction plate has a perforated suction lifting surface directed downward for contact with the upper surface of the article, an airflow suction system conveys vacuum air pressure to that surface, a lifter actuation system such as a robotic arm lifts and moves the plate, and an elongate bar movably mounted along an edge of the plate carries nozzles that are lowered to sweep a suction airflow across the surface beneath to remove dust or debris [REF:US-11247858-B2]. That system carries the article away from the work surface and cleans the work surface by suction; it does not deliver vibration into a covering element already laid on a bed of bonding material, and it accordingly says nothing about how a vibrating tool might be kept in contact with such a covering element while it is moved over it.

The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles reduce some of the vibration reaching the operator, but they do so by absorbing mechanical energy that would otherwise have gone into the covering element, so the tool is made kinder to the operator by being made worse at its job. The two problems are coupled: firmer coupling to the covering element is obtained by pressing harder, and pressing harder is exactly what increases the vibration dose to the operator.

input.summary: Two minor findings were reported and both are addressed. The Background topic sentence in paragraph 4 no longer attributes a compliant wall or an alternation between holding and moving to the group of three non-tile vacuum references; the lead-in is now a neutral statement that these arrangements approach holding a body against a surface in other ways, each on the terms of its own document, so the three reference-specific sentences that follow carry the whole of the characterization. The elastic partitions stay attributed only to US-11408462-B2, the suction-mode and blower-mode alternation only to US-10001245-B2, and the vibration-loosened suction travel only to US-4934475-A, matching what each file states. For the fluid-communication finding, the finding records that no text change is available from the present sources and that inventing a duct or opening is expressly out of bounds, so the claims, description and FIG. 2 are unchanged and the gap stands as flagged for the signing attorney. No claim, numeral, figure brief, drawing description, or embodiment was altered, and the numeral table and all five figure files remain synchronized with the text.
reasoning: The Background finding was about attribution, not about substance, so the repair had to remove the collective reading without weakening what the applicant says about any individual reference. I replaced only the lead-in sentence and left the three reference-specific sentences exactly as they were, since the review confirmed each of them describes its own document accurately.

I checked the trait claims against the files before rewriting. prior_art/US-10001245-B2.md describes its peripheral structure only as at least one cup-shaped portion depending from the second side and defining a cavity, with no material or elasticity stated, so a compliant wall cannot be attributed to it. prior_art/US-11408462-B2.md recites adhering, elastic partitions and a restricting member, with nothing about travelling along the wall surface, so alternation between holding and moving cannot be attributed to it. The rewritten lead-in asserts neither trait of anyone.

I chose the neutral lead-in rather than a split lead-in that names which reference supports which trait, because the following sentences already state each trait in its own reference's terms. Restating the traits in the lead-in would duplicate the characterization and create a second place where a distributive reading could go wrong.

The lead-in still does the paragraph's structural work of separating tile-setting devices from vacuum coupling used elsewhere, which is what the argument later depends on: none of these documents holds a tool down on a workpiece through a rigid non-sealing perimeter while sliding it, and the paragraph must set that up without overstating them.

For the fluid-communication finding I made no change, following the finding's own recorded resolution. The disclosure says only that the air-extraction mechanism is in fluid communication with a chamber located on the second side of the base, and an earlier corrective message expressly removed a through-base extraction opening and duct from this application. Adding any path now would be inventing structure from nothing and would reintroduce matter that was already stricken, so the claims, the detailed description and the deliberately broken indicating line in FIG. 2 stand as they are.

No drawing sheet was named in this report, so no figure brief was touched. FIG. 3's ring topology repair from the last turn stands, and the numeral table, the Brief Description of the Drawings, the detailed description and the five figure files remain in the same synchronized state the review verified.

The Background edit strengthens rather than weakens the footing for that position: by attributing the elastic partitions only to US-11408462-B2, the suction-mode and blower-mode alternation only to US-10001245-B2, and the vibration-loosened suction travel only to US-4934475-A, each distinction the claim relies on is now anchored to the document that actually supports it. DE-202021002652-U1 remains addressed in paragraph 3 for its rubber-elastic apron suction cups, and US-11247858-B2 remains addressed as lifting and cleaning equipment that does not deliver vibration into a laid covering element.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing

sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded

outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than

3	The draft is substantively source-faithful and internally consistent. Every independent and dependent claim limitation, every numbered part (10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42, 44, 46) and every embodiment detail traces to an exact affirmative passage in input/disclosure.md; none of the features the corrective QA message listed for deletion survives anywhere in the text, briefs or pixels. The five rendered sheets agree with their briefs, with the Brief Description of the Drawings and with the detailed description; each numeral labels one part everywhere it appears; the FIG. 2 (contact) versus FIG. 4 (clearance) section planes are expressly reconciled in the description; leaders do not cross. The four cited references are each described from their own claim text. Four minor items remain: an unshown, unexplained air path across the base (a gap inherited from the disclosure, not invented by the draft); one inferential clause appended to the US-10001245-B2 characterisation; FIG. 1 depicting handle 44 as a featureless block in an undisclosed position; and claim 1 omitting the "at the perimeter" placement that the disclosure and description always give the loop.
4	
5	## Reviewer findings
6	
7	- **[minor] Fluid communication across the rigid base is claimed and described but shown nowhere and explained nowhere** (draft/09-claims.md claims 1, 10 and 14; draft/08-detailed-description.md paras 7, 13, 23; draft/07-drawings.md FIG. 2 en) - Each independent claim requires the air-extraction mechanism, mounted on the first side, to be in fluid communication with the chamber on the opposite side of a base the specification insists is rigid and continuous. No passage of the description says how air crosses the base, and the only figure that addresses the air path deliberately breaks the indicating line at the base. I verified in rendered-FIG-2.png that the dashed line runs inside the housing (roughly y=225-280) and again in the chamber (roughly y=445-590) with no dashes crossing the hatched slab, exactly as the brief specifies: 'the broken line stops at the upper face of the base 12 and resumes below its lower face, no passage through the base 12 being drawn or asserted.' This is faithful drafting rather than an invented fact - the inventor's disclosure likewise says only 'is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base' and gives no route - so the correct response is not to draft a duct or opening (the corrective message expressly rejected both). Flagged for awareness so the signing attorney can decide whether to obtain one sentence from the inventor before filing.
8	  - Suggested fix: No text change is available from the present sources. Either leave as filed and record the gap, or ask the inventor for one sentence on how the extraction mechanism communicates with the chamber and, if answered, add it to the description and show it as a real path in FIG. 2.
9	- **[minor] Concluding clause about US-10001245-B2 states an inference rather than something the reference file says** (draft/05-background.md, paragraph 4 (sentence citing [REF:US-10001245-B2])) - The descriptive part of the sentence is accurate: prior_art/US-10001245-B2.md recites that the second side with the cavity 'is securely coupleable to a surface of the structure via a vacuum force induced by said at least one pneumatic generator in the suction mode' and 'is movable substantially frictionlessly across the surface via an air cushion induced by said at least one pneumatic generator in the blower mode'. The trailing clause 'so that the vacuum coupling is given up for the period during which the assembly is moved' is the drafter's conclusion; those words, and any statement that the vacuum is released or interrupted during movement, do not appear in the file. The inference is defensible, because claim 2 of the same file recites 'a control configured to selectively switch said at least one pneumatic generator between the suction mode and the blower mode', which implies the modes are alternatives; I therefore mark this minor rather than critical. But as an applicant characterisation of prior art it asserts a consequence the source itself never states.
10	  - Suggested fix: Either delete the trailing clause, or tie it to the words the file supplies, e.g. '...in a blower mode, the generator being selectively switched between the suction mode and the blower mode by a control [REF:US-10001245-B2].'
11	- **[minor] FIG. 1 depicts handle 44 as a featureless block on the top of the base, a form and mounting position the disclosure does not give** (figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md and figures/rendered-FIG-1.png; draft/08-detailed-descr) - In rendered-FIG-1.png the handle 44 is drawn as one closed rectangular block on the top face of the base, identical in form to the vibration motor 18 block on its left and the air-extraction mechanism 20 block on its right; nothing graspable is depicted. The inventor's disclosure says only that handles may be present and what they are for, with no form, number or location, and the description follows that restraint. The pixels therefore supply a mounting position (on the first side, between motor and pump) that no source states. The mitigation is real and deliberate: the brief records that 'the order and spacing of the three blocks is a placement convention for this sheet only, no particular handle form, size or mounting arrangement being asserted', the Brief Description says the handle is 'shown schematically', and the corrective message in input/conversation.md expressly rejected 'arbitrary bail-handle geometry'. No patent text was widened to match the geometry, so I mark this minor; it is noted because claim 8 recites a handle whose only depiction is an unmarked cube.
12	  - Suggested fix: No text change is required. If the inventor can confirm a handle form and location, depict it; otherwise leave the schematic block and consider carrying the brief's caveat into the FIG. 1 sentence of the Brief Description, which already says 'shown schematically'.
13	- **[minor] Claim 1 omits the 'at the perimeter of the second side' placement that the disclosure and description always give the loop** (draft/09-claims.md claim 1 (and the same wording in claims 10 and 14); compare draft/08-detailed-description.md para 29) - Claim 1 requires only that the perimeter member extend from the second side and surround a chamber located on the second side. - **[minor] Fluid communication across the rigid base is claimed and described but shown nowhere and explained nowhere** (draft/09-claims.md claims 1, 10 and 14; draft/08-detailed-description.md paras 7, 13, 23; draft/07-drawings.md FIG. 2 en) - Each independent claim requires the air-extraction mechanism, mounted on the first side, to be in fluid communication with the chamber on the opposite side of a base the specification insists is rigid and continuous. No passage of the description says how air crosses the base, and the only figure that addresses the air path deliberately breaks the indicating line at the base. I verified in rendered-FIG-2.png that the dashed line runs inside the housing (roughly y=225-280) and again in the chamber (roughly y=445-590) with no dashes crossing the hatched slab, exactly as the brief specifies: 'the broken line stops at the upper face of the base 12 and resumes below its lower face, no passage through the base 12 being drawn or asserted.' This is faithful drafting rather than an invented fact - the inventor's disclosure likewise says only 'is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base' and gives no route - so the correct response is not to draft a duct or opening (the corrective message expressly rejected both). Flagged for awareness so the signing attorney can decide whether to obtain one sentence from the inventor before filing.
  - Suggested fix: No text change is available from the present sources. Either leave as filed and record the gap, or ask the inventor for one sentence on how the extraction mechanism communicates with the chamber and, if answered, add it to the description and show it as a real path in FIG. 2.
- **[minor] Concluding clause about US-10001245-B2 states an inference rather than something the reference file says** (draft/05-background.md, paragraph 4 (sentence citing [REF:US-10001245-B2])) - The descriptive part of the sentence is accurate: prior_art/US-10001245-B2.md recites that the second side with the cavity 'is securely coupleable to a surface of the structure via a vacuum force induced by said at least one pneumatic generator in the suction mode' and 'is movable substantially frictionlessly across the surface via an air cushion induced by said at least one pneumatic generator in the blower mode'. The trailing clause 'so that the vacuum coupling is given up for the period during which the assembly is moved' is the drafter's conclusion; those words, and any statement that the vacuum is released or interrupted during movement, do not appear in the file. The inference is defensible, because claim 2 of the same file recites 'a control configured to selectively switch said at least one pneumatic generator between the suction mode and the blower mode', which implies the modes are alternatives; I therefore mark this minor rather than critical. But as an applicant characterisation of prior art it asserts a consequence the source itself never states.
  - Suggested fix: Either delete the trailing clause, or tie it to the words the file supplies, e.g. '...in a blower mode, the generator being selectively switched between the suction mode and the blower mode by a control [REF:US-10001245-B2].'
- **[minor] FIG. 1 depicts handle 44 as a featureless block on the top of the base, a form and mounting position the disclosure does not give** (figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md and figures/rendered-FIG-1.png; draft/08-detailed-descr) - In rendered-FIG-1.png the handle 44 is drawn as one closed rectangular block on the top face of the base, identical in form to the vibration motor 18 block on its left and the air-extraction mechanism 20 block on its right; nothing graspable is depicted. The inventor's disclosure says only that handles may be present and what they are for, with no form, number or location, and the description follows that restraint. The pixels therefore supply a mounting position (on the first side, between motor and pump) that no source states. The mitigation is real and deliberate: the brief records that 'the order and spacing of the three blocks is a placement convention for this sheet only, no particular handle form, size or mounting arrangement being asserted', the Brief Description says the handle is 'shown schematically', and the corrective message in input/conversation.md expressly rejected 'arbitrary bail-handle geometry'. No patent text was widened to match the geometry, so I mark this minor; it is noted because claim 8 recites a handle whose only depiction is an unmarked cube.
  - Suggested fix: No text change is required. If the inventor can confirm a handle form and location, depict it; otherwise leave the schematic block and consider carrying the brief's caveat into the FIG. 1 sentence of the Brief Description, which already says 'shown schematically'.
- **[minor] Claim 1 omits the 'at the perimeter of the second side' placement that the disclosure and description always give the loop** (draft/09-claims.md claim 1 (and the same wording in claims 10 and 14); compare draft/08-detailed-description.md para 29) - Claim 1 requires only that the perimeter member extend from the second side and surround a chamber located on the second side. The disclosure places the loop at the perimeter of the second side, and the description does so consistently. As drafted, claim 1 also reads on a loop standing inboard of the base edge, an arrangement neither source describes. The gap is small - the element is named 'perimeter member', and claim 2 recites the perimeter placement expressly as a fallback - so I mark this minor rather than critical, but it is a drift between the claim and the description of the same element that a reviewer should see before filing.
  - Suggested fix: If the broader recitation is not wanted, move the claim 2 language into claim 1 ('...extending from the second side at a perimeter thereof and surrounding a chamber...'); otherwise leave claim 1 and claim 2 as the intended ladder and record the deliberate generalisation.

Fix every listed item before returning. If an advisory is a false positive, make
the wording or figure specification unambiguous enough that the check passes.

1	A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials, and the bearing face is the end face of that member.
2	
3	The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.
4	
5	Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator need not press the device against the covering element, and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is avoided rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base and the perimeter member terminating in the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. The device is thus coupled to the covering element without an intervening compliant member or air film, while the operator's hands carry less.
6	
7	Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.
8	
9	In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.
10	
11	A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.
12

A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials, and the bearing face is the end face of that member.

The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.

Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator need not press the device against the covering element, and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is avoided rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base and the perimeter member terminating in the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. The device is thus coupled to the covering element without an intervening compliant member or air film, while the operator's hands carry less.

Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.

In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.

A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.

27	The perimeter member and the chamber
28	
29	A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.
30	
31	The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.
32	
33	The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.
34	
35	Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of the perimeter member 24, taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.
36	
37	The pressure differential that holds the device down
38	
39	The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.
40	
41	The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.
42	
43	The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.
44	
45	The vibration transmission path
46	
47	The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.
48	
49	The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.
50	
51	The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.
52	
53	The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of the perimeter member 24, taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

When a tile or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.

Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place. In one known hand-held device for lifting and laying tiles, a handle carries two shafts, an electric motor vibrates the shafts, and a head shell at the free end of each shaft carries a suction cup on its underside, the suction cups being evacuated by an electrically operated pump and each being formed by a rubber-elastic apron [REF:DE-202021002652-U1].

Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.

Vacuum coupling arrangements used away from tile setting approach the holding of a body against a surface in other ways, each on the terms of its own document. In one adhesion device that holds itself to a wall surface, the peripheral wall of the decompressed space between the base and the wall surface is formed by elastic partitions, of which the partition nearer the wall surface has an end that contacts the wall surface, and a frame member of higher rigidity is added on the partition to restrict the partition from being deformed into that space as it is drawn down [REF:US-11408462-B2]. In a base assembly for coupling an end effector to a structure, a cavity on the second side of the assembly is held to the structure by vacuum drawn by a pneumatic generator operating in a suction mode, and the assembly is moved across the structure substantially frictionlessly on an air cushion produced by the same generator operating in a blower mode [REF:US-10001245-B2], so that the vacuum coupling is given up for the period during which the assembly is moved. In a device that suction-adheres to a wall surface and moves along it, a seal member mounted in the main body defines a pressure reduction space in cooperation with the wall surface, vacuum creating means discharges fluid from that space so that the main body adheres by the difference in fluid pressure inside and outside the space, and vibration generating means mounted on the main body imparts a lifting force in a direction away from the wall surface that reduces the suction-adhering force, together with a force along the wall surface that moves the main body [REF:US-4934475-A]. The vibration there is used to loosen the suction-adhering hold and to drive the main body along the wall surface. Vacuum is used differently again in handling equipment, where the object is to pick a workpiece up rather than to hold a tool down on it: in one vacuum plate lifting system for lifting sheet material articles, a substantially horizontal suction plate has a perforated suction lifting surface directed downward for contact with the upper surface of the article, an airflow suction system conveys vacuum air pressure to that surface, a lifter actuation system such as a robotic arm lifts and moves the plate, and an elongate bar movably mounted along an edge of the plate carries nozzles that are lowered to sweep a suction airflow across the surface beneath to remove dust or debris [REF:US-11247858-B2]. That system carries the article away from the work surface and cleans the work surface by suction; it does not deliver vibration into a covering element already laid on a bed of bonding material, and it accordingly says nothing about how a vibrating tool might be kept in contact with such a covering element while it is moved over it.

The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles reduce some of the vibration reaching the operator, but they do so by absorbing mechanical energy that would otherwise have gone into the covering element, so the tool is made kinder to the operator by being made worse at its job. The two problems are coupled: firmer coupling to the covering element is obtained by pressing harder, and pressing harder is exactly what increases the vibration dose to the operator.

What is needed is a way to hold a vibration device against a covering element with a force that does not come from the operator's arms, to conduct the vibration into the covering element without passing it through any compliant member, and to allow the device to be moved from area to area over the covering element without ever giving up that hold.

a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side;

a vibration motor coupled to the first side;

a perimeter member extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, the perimeter member being rigid and of a low-friction material and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face that is an end face of the perimeter member, the chamber being bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and, when the bearing face is placed against an exposed face of the covering element, by the exposed face, and a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber; and

an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber, the air-extraction mechanism being operable to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while the ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, a resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device against the covering element;

wherein a vibration transmission path from the vibration motor to the bearing face passes through the base and the perimeter member, each member of the vibration transmission path is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

wherein the bearing face is slidable over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained.

a vibration device comprising a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side, a vibration motor coupled to the first side, a perimeter member extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, and an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber,

whereby a position of the vibration device over the exposed face is controlled by tension applied to the flexible pulling element while a force holding the vibration device against the covering element is supplied independently of the flexible pulling element by the pressure differential.

11. The system of claim 10, wherein the flexible pulling element is a rope, a wire or a cable.
