placing a vibration device on an exposed face of the covering element that has been laid on the bonding material, the vibration device comprising a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side, a vibration motor coupled to the first side, a rigid perimeter member of a low-friction material extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side and terminating in a bearing face that is an end face of the perimeter member, and an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber, whereby the bearing face is brought against the exposed face so that the chamber is bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and the exposed face, with a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face;

operating the air-extraction mechanism to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, and holding the vibration device against the covering element by a resulting pressure differential;

operating the vibration motor and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor to the covering element along a vibration transmission path passing through the base and the perimeter member to the bearing face, each member of the vibration transmission path being rigid and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount being interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

translating the vibration device across the exposed face, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face over the exposed face, so that the vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element.

15. The method of claim 14, wherein the pressure differential is maintained continuously while the vibration device is translated across the exposed face, so that the vibration device is held against the covering element and slid over the exposed face at the same time.

16. The method of claim 14, wherein the vibration device is translated across the exposed face by applying tension to a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device.

17. The method of claim 14, wherein the vibration device is translated across the exposed face by guiding the vibration device with a handle, and wherein the pressure differential holds the vibration device against the covering element without a downward force being required from an operator.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials, and the bearing face is the end face of that member.

The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.

Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator need not press the device against the covering element, and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is avoided rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base and the perimeter member terminating in the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. The device is thus coupled to the covering element without an intervening compliant member or air film, while the operator's hands carry less.

Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.

In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.

A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.

A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The US-10001245-B2 sentence in the Background now ends with the file's own recitation of a control that selectively switches the pneumatic generator between the suction mode and the blower mode, replacing the drafter's inference that the vacuum coupling is given up while the assembly moves. Claim 1 now recites the perimeter member as extending from the second side at a perimeter thereof, and the same placement was added to the corresponding elements of system claim 10 and method claim 14, closing the drift from the description; claim 2, whose only limitation had been that placement, now carries the disclosed non-sealing character of the closed loop, so the ladder keeps a real fallback instead of a duplicate. The Summary and the overview paragraph of the detailed description were brought into the same words. For the handle depiction, the FIG. 1 sentence of the Brief Description and the Handles paragraph now state that no particular form, number or mounting position of the handle is asserted by the schematic block in FIG. 1. The unshown air path across the base is left exactly as filed, which is the resolution the finding records, since no source states a route and a through-base opening and duct were expressly struck from this application earlier. No figure brief was edited, so the five certified sheets stand, and the numeral table is unchanged.
reasoning: The Background clause was fixed by substituting source text for inference. The file recites a control configured to selectively switch the generator between suction mode and blower mode, so the sentence now ends on that recitation and asserts no consequence about the vacuum being released. The distinction the application relies on, that this reference moves the assembly on a blower-fed air cushion rather than sliding while a differential is held, is still carried by the descriptive part of the same sentence, which the review confirmed as accurate.

On the claim placement, I took the reviewer's first option and moved the perimeter placement into claim 1 rather than recording a deliberate generalization. The disclosure states that the perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt, so the loop is always at the perimeter; a claim reading on a loop standing inboard of the base edge was claiming something no source describes, which is a written-description exposure rather than useful breadth.

Adding that placement to claim 1 made the old claim 2 a duplicate, which would have created a new defect while curing the reported one. I rewrote claim 2 on the disclosed non-sealing character: the closed loop restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber through the clearance without closing the clearance and without forming a complete airtight seal. That is drawn from the description's own words at paragraphs 33 and 35 and is worth more as a fallback than the placement was, because it is the feature that separates the perimeter member from a suction cup or a compliant sealing skirt.

I carried the placement into claims 10 and 14 because the finding names them as carrying the same wording, and independent claims in different statutory classes should not diverge on the same recited element.

Claim language must appear in the description in the same words, so I aligned the Summary and the overview paragraph of the detailed description to say the perimeter member extends from the second side at a perimeter of that side and runs around the chamber. Paragraph 29 already stated the perimeter placement; the two other passages now match rather than merely being consistent with it.

For the handle, no form or location is disclosed, so the answer was to disclaim what the schematic block might otherwise imply rather than to draw a handle the sources do not describe. The Brief Description's FIG. 1 sentence and the Handles paragraph now both say that the depiction asserts no particular form, number or mounting position, which puts the caveat in the patent text where it governs, not only in the figure brief. Claim 8 continues to recite the handle functionally, as the disclosure does.

I made no change for the fluid communication across the base and did not touch claims 1, 10 or 14 on that point, the description paragraphs, or FIG. 2. The disclosure says only that the air-extraction mechanism is in fluid communication with a chamber located on the second side of the base, and an earlier corrective instruction removed a through-base extraction opening and duct from this application, so there is no source from which a path could be written or drawn.

No file in figures/ was edited, deliberately: the report confirmed the five rendered sheets agree with their briefs and with the text, and the text edits I made are disclaimers and claim wording that change nothing a sheet depicts, so there was no reason to force a re-render of certified geometry.

input.prior_art_strategy: Claim 1 still turns on the same combination: a rigid, low-friction perimeter member, now expressly at the perimeter of the second side, ending in a bearing face that leaves a clearance through which ambient air enters continuously; an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric rate holds the chamber below atmospheric against that continuous ingress; an all-rigid transmission path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. Adding the perimeter placement narrows nothing the art teaches, since none of these references discloses a non-sealing rigid perimeter that slides under a sustained differential wherever it is placed. The rewritten claim 2 now expressly recites the non-sealing, flow-restricting loop, which is the cleanest separation from DE-202021002652-U1 and US-11408462-B2, whose holding structures are a rubber-elastic apron and elastic partitions that seal and damp. US-10001245-B2 remains distinguished by its switch between a suction mode that holds and a blower mode that floats the assembly on an air cushion, now described strictly in the words of its own claims. US-4934475-A remains distinguished as travelling by vibration that reduces the suction-adhering force, and US-11247858-B2 as lifting and cleaning equipment that delivers no vibration into a laid covering element.

The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

input.summary: Both findings are fixed. Claim 2 now recites "restricting a flow of the ambient air into the chamber through the clearance", which takes its antecedent from the ambient air already recited in claim 1 and clears the antecedent-basis check. The FIG. 2 brief now places the two cut legs of the loop one at each end of the slab with the outer side of each leg flush with the corresponding end, so the loop runs at the perimeter of the underside, matching the description and the ring of FIG. 3; the sheet regenerates from that brief. To hold the brief within the length limit I removed two redundant clauses from it: the sentence repeating that the slab's lower face meets the legs, which line 7 and the numeral 24 entry both already state, and the trailing endpoint modifier on numeral 12, leaving the broader interior target. No patent text was changed for the drawing finding, and the numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description and other four figure briefs are untouched.
reasoning: Claim 2's gap was purely an article. Claim 1 recites that ambient air enters the chamber through the clearance but never names a flow, so 'the flow' pointed at nothing. Changing it to 'a flow of the ambient air' introduces the flow in claim 2 while tying it to the ambient air of claim 1, so the limitation's substance, which the description supports at the passage about the perimeter member restricting the flow of ambient air into the chamber without closing that path, is unchanged.

The FIG. 2 disagreement was a drawing defect, not a text problem, so the repair went into the figure brief and the description stayed as written. The description states twice that the perimeter member stands at the perimeter of the second side, and FIG. 3 draws the ring's outer edge as the outer boundary of the underside; the rendered section had the base overhanging the loop on both sides, which contradicts both. The brief now states the flush relationship positively, as physical geometry rather than as a rendering prohibition.

Adding that clause pushed the brief to 2885 characters, over the limit, so I paid for it by deleting two clauses that carried no unique information. The slab-to-leg contact survives in the opening sentence, which has the legs hanging from the underside of the slab, and in the numeral 24 entry, which has the loop hanging from the lower edge of the base 12. The numeral 12 endpoint is now simply well inside the hatching, which is the broad interior target the endpoint guidance prefers over the extra away-from-the-edge-lines modifier.

I did not touch anything else in FIG. 2. The broken indicating line still stops at the upper face and resumes below the lower face with no passage through the base asserted, which is what keeps the sheet faithful to a disclosure that gives no route across the base, and the numerals on the sheet are unchanged so the figure plan and the table stay in step.
The other four briefs were left alone because no finding touches them and editing a certified brief would force an unnecessary re-render.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged. Claim 1 still rests on the rigid low-friction perimeter member at the perimeter of the second side, ending in a bearing face that leaves a clearance admitting ambient air continuously; an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric rate holds the chamber below atmospheric against that continuous ingress; an all-rigid transmission path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. Claim 2 keeps the non-sealing, flow-restricting closed loop, with only the article corrected, which is the limitation that most directly separates the invention from the rubber-elastic apron of DE-202021002652-U1 and the elastic partitions of US-11408462-B2. input.summary: The single finding is fixed in the FIG. 2 brief only. The sentence that asked for hatching "at a different angle from that of the bodies it touches" is replaced by an explicit per-body assignment: the base 12 slab is hatched rising to the right at about 45 degrees, both legs of the perimeter member 24 falling to the right at about 45 degrees, and the covering element 36 band rising to the right at about 75 degrees. That makes the base/leg boundary and the leg/tile contact, which is the rigid contact interface the description turns on, visually separable when the sheet regenerates. To keep the brief inside the length limit I compressed three passages without dropping any required body, contact or relationship. No patent text, claim, numeral definition, drawing description, or other figure brief was touched, and the flush perimeter placement added in the previous round is preserved.
reasoning: The defect was that the brief stated the hatching requirement relationally, as an angle different from the touching body, which left the renderer free to satisfy it in name while drawing all three cut bodies at the same slope. Naming an absolute direction for each body removes the discretion, and FIG. 4 already demonstrates that the renderer varies slope when the brief assigns them, so this is the form of instruction that works here.

I assigned the angles so that the two interfaces that matter are the ones most strongly separated: the slab rises to the right and the legs fall to the right, so the base and the perimeter member cross at their boundary, and the band rises at a markedly steeper slope than the legs, so the bearing contact with the covering element reads as a boundary between two different bodies rather than as continuous material.

Hatch direction is a sectioning convention, not invention geometry, so specifying degrees here adds nothing to the disclosure. The bodies, their contacts and their placement are unchanged, and the brief still marks every body as shown schematically.

The explicit assignment is longer than the sentence it replaces, so I paid for it inside the same brief rather than letting it exceed the length limit: I dropped a trailing summary clause that merely restated the three angles, shortened the housing's endpoint entry, and kept the earlier compressions. Every body, contact, opening and the broken indicating line survive intact.

I preserved the flush relationship from the previous round, with the outer side of each leg at the corresponding end of the slab so the loop runs at the perimeter of the underside, because that is what reconciles FIG. 2 with the description and with the ring of FIG. 3.

The broken line still stops at the upper face of the base 12 and resumes below its lower face with no passage asserted, which keeps the sheet faithful to a disclosure that gives no route across the base. Numerals 12, 14, 20, 22, 24 and 36 are unchanged, so the sheet, the numeral table and the Brief Description remain in step, and no other figure brief was edited so the other four sheets stay as certified.

1. A vibration device for bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the vibration device comprising:

a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side;

a vibration motor coupled to the first side;

a perimeter member extending from the second side at a perimeter thereof and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, the perimeter member being rigid and of a low-friction material and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face that is an end face of the perimeter member, the chamber being bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and, when the bearing face is placed against an exposed face of the covering element, by the exposed face, and a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber; and

an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber, the air-extraction mechanism being operable to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while the ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, a resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device against the covering element;

wherein a vibration transmission path from the vibration motor to the bearing face passes through the base and the perimeter member, each member of the vibration transmission path is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

wherein the bearing face is slidable over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained.

2. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the perimeter member is a closed loop that runs around the chamber, the closed loop restricting a flow of the ambient air into the chamber through the clearance without closing the clearance and without forming a complete airtight seal.

3. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the low-friction material of the perimeter member is plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

4. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the perimeter member is free of rubber, elastomer and foam, and makes rigid contact with the exposed face.

a vibration device comprising a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side, a vibration motor coupled to the first side, a perimeter member extending from the second side at a perimeter thereof and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, and an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber,

translating the vibration device across the exposed face, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face over the exposed face, so that the vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element.

input.summary: Both findings are drawing-side and both are fixed without touching the patent text. In the FIG. 1 brief the two block assignments now read left to right as vibration motor 18, air-extraction mechanism 20, handle 44, with the bullets amended to match, so the brief and the sheet agree on which numeral belongs to which block; the sentence declaring the order and spacing a per-sheet placement convention is retained unchanged. In the FIG. 2 brief the prescribed hatching is unchanged in substance but the leg direction is now stated twice over, falling to the right at about 45 degrees and running from upper left down to lower right, so the sheet regenerates with the perimeter member 24 legs crossing the base 12 hatching rather than parallel to it. Adding that clause pushed the brief past the length limit, so I compressed four short phrases that repeated information already carried elsewhere in the same brief, leaving it at 2792 characters with every body, contact and relationship intact. The claims, description, Brief Description of the Drawings, numeral table and the other three briefs are untouched.
reasoning: For FIG. 1 the mismatch was between a brief and a sheet on a point with no technical content: the three blocks are identical plain outlines and the brief itself declares their order a per-sheet placement convention. The patent text says nothing about where the handle sits relative to the air-extraction mechanism, and both are on the first side either way, so aligning the brief's assignment with the rendered leaders resolves the inconsistency without adding, widening, or moving anything in the disclosure.

I applied the swap in all three places it appears, the geometry sentence and both bullets, so the brief cannot be read two ways: 20 is now the middle block standing between the other two, and 44 is the right-hand block. The numeral list for the sheet is unchanged, so the union of per-sheet numerals still equals the table.

For FIG. 2 the brief was already right and the render did not follow it, so I did not weaken the requirement to match the pixels. I strengthened it instead, giving the leg direction in two equivalent forms so an image model has no room to read falling to the right as a rising slope. The base stays rising to the right and the band stays at about 75 degrees, so the base to leg boundary and the leg to tile contact both read as boundaries between separate parts, which is what the description requires of a perimeter member standing proud of the second side and rigidly connected to the base.

That addition took the brief over the length limit, so I paid for it inside the same file rather than dropping geometry: the housing is described as standing on the slab, which the later sentence about the upper face already locates; the legs are described once as hatched rather than twice; and the broken-line sentence keeps its substance, that the line stops at the upper face and resumes below the lower face with no passage through the base asserted.

I left the FIG. 2 numerals, endpoint targets, flush perimeter placement and the broken indicating line exactly as they were, since none of those was in question and each is load-bearing: the flush placement reconciles this sheet with the description and with the ring of FIG. 3, and the broken line keeps the sheet faithful to a disclosure that gives no route across the base.

No file in draft/ was edited. Neither finding implicated the claims, the description, the Brief Description of the Drawings or the numeral table, and the FIG. 1 block order is not stated in any of them, so there was nothing to resynchronize.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged, and the FIG. 2 repair supports it. Claim 1 rests on the rigid low-friction perimeter member at the perimeter of the second side, ending in a bearing face that leaves a clearance admitting ambient air continuously; an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric rate holds the chamber below atmospheric against that ingress; an all-rigid transmission path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. Hatching that distinguishes the base from the perimeter member keeps the section reading as two rigid parts rigidly connected, which is the structure that separates the invention from the rubber-elastic apron of DE-202021002652-U1 and the elastic partitions of US-11408462-B2. US-10001245-B2 remains distinguished by its control switching between a suction mode that holds and a blower mode that floats the assembly, US-4934475-A by travel driven by vibration that reduces the suction-adhering force, and US-11247858-B2 as lifting and cleaning equipment that delivers no vibration into a laid covering element.

Hatching that distinguishes the base from the perimeter member keeps the section reading as two rigid parts rigidly connected, which is the structure that separates the invention from the rubber-elastic apron of DE-202021002652-U1 and the elastic partitions of US-11408462-B2. US-10001245-B2 remains distinguished by its control switching between a suction mode that holds and a blower mode that floats the assembly, US-4934475-A by travel driven by vibration that reduces the suction-adhering force, and US-11247858-B2 as lifting and cleaning equipment that delivers no vibration into a laid covering element.
data.answer: Both defects are drawing-side and both are now handled in the figure briefs, with no change to the claims, description, Brief Description of the Drawings or numeral table. FIG. 1's brief now assigns the three blocks left to right as vibration motor 18, air-extraction mechanism 20, handle 44, and the two bullets were amended to match, so the brief and the rendered leaders agree. Nothing about the invention turns on that order: the blocks are identical plain outlines, the brief still declares their order and spacing a per-sheet placement convention with no handle form, size or mounting arrangement asserted, and the patent text is silent on where the handle sits relative to the air-extraction mechanism, both being on the first side of the base either way. For FIG. 2 I kept the requirement and made it harder to misread rather than relaxing it: the legs of the perimeter member 24 are now specified as hatched falling to the right at about 45 degrees, running from upper left down to lower right, while the base 12 keeps hatching rising to the right and the covering element 36 keeps about 75 degrees. The base to leg boundary and the leg to tile contact therefore read as boundaries between separate parts when the sheet regenerates, which is what the description requires of a perimeter member standing proud of the second side and rigidly connected to the base. That clause took the brief past the length limit, so I compressed four phrases that repeated information already present, leaving 2792 characters with every body, contact, opening and the broken indicating line intact, including the flush placement of the loop at the perimeter of the underside and the line that stops at the base faces without asserting a passage. Sheet numeral lists are unchanged, so the briefs, the table and the text remain synchronized.

Numerals 10-46 each label one part consistently across numerals.md, the description, the briefs and the printed sheets, and every figure statement in the description matches what the corresponding image actually contains. The only defects I found are in rendered hatching: FIG. 2 as rendered does not carry the three distinct section linings its brief specifies, and in FIG. 4 the perimeter-member column and the covering-element band appear to share one angle. Both are repairable by re-rendering from the existing, already-correct briefs; no text change is needed.

6	
7	- **[major] Rendered FIG. 2 does not carry the three distinct section linings its brief specifies; base 12, perimeter member 24 and covering element 36 are hatched identically** (figures/rendered-FIG-2.png, compared with figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-CHAMBER.md ("Geometry to be drawn",) - The brief prescribes three different section linings for the three cut bodies. In the rendered sheet all three appear to carry one and the same lining: parallel strokes at roughly 45 degrees rising to the right (y decreasing as x increases). Concrete pixel relationships: (a) along the shared junction at the underside of the slab, where each leg hangs from the base, the strokes above the junction and the strokes below it run in the same up-to-the-right sense at the same slope, so they read as continuing across the junction instead of forming the mirrored V that a 45-degrees-rising / 45-degrees-falling pair would produce; (b) at the top boundary of the bottom band, where each leg stands on the covering element, the leg strokes and the band strokes are likewise parallel at about 45 degrees, whereas a 45-degree leg meeting a 75-degree band would show a clear change of slope and stroke density across that line. The consequence is that the base, the perimeter member and the tile - three separate parts the specification is at pains to distinguish ("The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16") - are visually indistinguishable in the one sectional view. Reconciling with review/figure-audit-evidence.json: the FIG. 2 "geometry" summary asserts the three angles, but it restates the brief's wording verbatim ("rising to the right at about 45 degrees", "falling to the right at about 45 degrees", "about 75 degrees rising to the right"), which is specification echo rather than measurement; the pixel-exact evidence recorded for this sheet (OCR, leader routing, marked endpoints at (700,290), (470,222), (804,150), (499,475), (1140,475), (700,690)) tests numerals and terminal dots only and says nothing about hatch angle, so no measured evidence contradicts this reading. That the renderer can produce distinct angles is shown by FIG. 4, where the middle band is visibly much steeper than the bands above and below it. I am confident about the direction of the leg hatching; my estimate of the band's angle is less precise, but it is plainly nowhere near the near-vertical 75 degrees called for.
8	  - Suggested fix: Re-render rendered-FIG-2.png from the unchanged brief so that the two legs of the perimeter member are hatched falling to the right (y increasing as x increases) at about 45 degrees and the covering-element band is hatched rising to the right at about 75 degrees, leaving the base slab rising to the right at about 45 degrees. No change to the patent text, claims, numeral table or brief is required.
9	- **[minor] In rendered FIG. 4 the perimeter-member column and the covering-element band appear to share one hatch angle, contrary to the brief** (figures/rendered-FIG-4.png, compared with figures/FIG-4-ENLARGED-SECTION-OF-THE-PERIMETER-MEMBER-END.md ("Geometry to be) - The brief requires the column's hatching to differ in angle from the uppermost band beneath it. In the rendered sheet the column's strokes and the uppermost band's strokes both rise to the right at what looks like the same slope (each crosses its body's full height with a horizontal run of roughly the same magnitude as that height times the same factor), so the perimeter member and the covering element read as the same lining, while the middle band (bonding material) is plainly steeper and the lowest band (substrate) plainly shallower. I mark this minor because the two bodies are separated by the clearance rather than in contact, and because my angular estimate of two similar diagonals is less certain than a direction judgement.

input.summary: Both findings concern section lining in rendered sheets, and both are fixed by making each brief state the linings in terms an image model follows, without changing the invention. FIG. 2 now describes the base 12 slab as hatched sloping up to the right at about 45 degrees, both legs of the perimeter member 24 as sloping down to the right at about 45 degrees, the opposite slope to the slab's so the two linings meet in a V at the junction, and the covering element 36 band as steep, close to upright and leaning to the right. FIG. 4 previously specified its linings only by comparison with the neighbouring body, which is the wording that failed on FIG. 2, so each body now has its own assignment: the perimeter member 24 column sloping down to the right at about 45 degrees, the covering element 36 band sloping up to the right at about 45 degrees, the bonding material 40 band steep and close to upright, and the substrate 42 band at a shallow rising slope. Both briefs stay within the length limit, at 2799 and 2788 characters, paid for by compressing phrases that repeated information already carried elsewhere in the same brief. No patent text, claim, numeral definition, numeral list, or drawing description was changed.
reasoning: The FIG. 2 brief already prescribed three distinct angles and the render ignored them, so I did not relax the requirement to match the pixels. I changed how it is expressed: degrees alone were not enough, so each lining is now given as a direction of slope in plain visual terms, up to the right or down to the right, with the steep band described as close to upright rather than by an angle alone.

I added one relational cue that describes what the sheet must show rather than banning anything: where the legs hang from the slab, the two linings meet in a V at the junction. That is the exact feature the review looked for and could not find, so stating it positively gives both the renderer and the next inspection the same target.

FIG. 4 had the weaker form of the same instruction, hatching at an angle different from the band it lies against, which is satisfiable in name while everything is drawn alike. Since that phrasing is what produced the FIG. 2 failure, I replaced it in FIG. 4 with an explicit per-body assignment before it fails again, and set the column opposite in sense to the band beneath it so the perimeter member and the covering element cannot read as one lining.

The angle assignments carry no technical content. Section lining is a drawing convention; the bodies, their contacts, the clearance between the bearing face and the exposed face, and the layer order are unchanged, and each brief still declares its rectangular forms a per-sheet convention.

Both additions were longer than the text they replaced, so I paid for them inside the same files rather than exceeding the limit: in FIG. 2 the leg placement, the housing location, the chamber endpoint and the broken-line sentence lost words that other sentences already supply; in FIG. 4 I dropped a sentence requiring two lines that the numeral entries for the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 already require, and trimmed two endpoint modifiers to broader interior targets.

I preserved everything load-bearing on both sheets: the flush placement of the loop at the perimeter of the underside, the broken line stopping at the upper face of the base 12 and resuming below the lower face with no passage asserted, the enlarged open clearance in FIG. 4, and every numeral and endpoint. Sheet numeral lists are unchanged, so the briefs, the numeral table and the text remain synchronized and the other three sheets need no regeneration.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged, and both repairs serve it. Claim 1 rests on the rigid low-friction perimeter member at the perimeter of the second side, ending in a bearing face that leaves a clearance admitting ambient air continuously; an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric rate holds the chamber below atmospheric against that ingress; an all-rigid transmission path from motor to bearing face with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. Section lining that separates the base from the perimeter member, and the perimeter member from the covering element, keeps the drawings showing two rigid parts rigidly connected and bearing on the tile, which is the structure that distinguishes the invention from the rubber-elastic apron of DE-202021002652-U1 and the elastic partitions of US-11408462-B2. US-10001245-B2 remains distinguished by its control switching between a suction mode that holds and a blower mode that floats the assembly, US-4934475-A by travel driven by vibration that reduces the suction-adhering force, and US-11247858-B2 as lifting and cleaning equipment that delivers no vibration into a laid covering element.

Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

toolUseResult.newString: The first of two problems with existing tile vibration devices is that both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly.
toolUseResult.originalFile:
When a tile or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.

Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place. In one known hand-held device for lifting and laying tiles, a handle carries two shafts, an electric motor vibrates the shafts, and a head shell at the free end of each shaft carries a suction cup on its underside, the suction cups being evacuated by an electrically operated pump and each being formed by a rubber-elastic apron [REF:DE-202021002652-U1].

Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.

Vacuum coupling arrangements used away from tile setting approach the holding of a body against a surface in other ways, each on the terms of its own document. In one adhesion device that holds itself to a wall surface, the peripheral wall of the decompressed space between the base and the wall surface is formed by elastic partitions, of which the partition nearer the wall surface has an end that contacts the wall surface, and a frame member of higher rigidity is added on the partition to restrict the partition from being deformed into that space as it is drawn down [REF:US-11408462-B2]. In a base assembly for coupling an end effector to a structure, a cavity on the second side of the assembly is held to the structure by vacuum drawn by a pneumatic generator operating in a suction mode, and the assembly is moved across the structure substantially frictionlessly on an air cushion produced by the same generator operating in a blower mode, a control being provided that selectively switches the generator between the suction mode and the blower mode [REF:US-10001245-B2]. In a device that suction-adheres to a wall surface and moves along it, a seal member mounted in the main body defines a pressure reduction space in cooperation with the wall surface, vacuum creating means discharges fluid from that space so that the main body adheres by the difference in fluid pressure inside and outside the space, and vibration generating means mounted on the main body imparts a lifting force in a direction away from the wall surface that reduces the suction-adhering force, together with a force along the wall surface that moves the main body [REF:US-4934475-A]. The vibration there is used to loosen the suction-adhering hold and to drive the main body along the wall surface. Vacuum is used differently again in handling equipment, where the object is to pick a workpiece up rather than to hold a tool down on it: in one vacuum plate lifting system for lifting sheet material articles, a substantially horizontal suction plate has a perforated suction lifting surface directed downward for contact with the upper surface of the article, an airflow suction system conveys vacuum air pressure to that surface, a lifter actuation system such as a robotic arm lifts and moves the plate, and an elongate bar movably mounted along an edge of the plate carries nozzles that are lowered to sweep a suction airflow across the surface beneath to remove dust or debris [REF:US-11247858-B2]. That system carries the article away from the work surface and cleans the work surface by suction; it does not deliver vibration into a covering element already laid on a bed of bonding material, and it accordingly says nothing about how a vibrating tool might be kept in contact with such a covering element while it is moved over it.

The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles reduce some of the vibration reaching the operator, but they do so by absorbing mechanical energy that would otherwise have gone into the covering element, so the tool is made kinder to the operator by being made worse at its job. The two problems are coupled: firmer coupling to the covering element is obtained by pressing harder, and pressing harder is exactly what increases the vibration dose to the operator.

What is needed is a way to hold a vibration device against a covering element with a force that does not come from the operator's arms, to conduct the vibration into the covering element without passing it through any compliant member, and to allow the device to be moved from area to area over the covering element without ever giving up that hold.

content.content:
1	A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side at a perimeter of that side, runs around the chamber, and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials, and the bearing face is the end face of that member.
2	
3	The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side at a perimeter of that side, runs around the chamber, and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials, and the bearing face is the end face of that member.

The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.

Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator need not press the device against the covering element, and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is avoided rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base and the perimeter member terminating in the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. The device is thus coupled to the covering element without an intervening compliant member or air film, while the operator's hands carry less.

Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.

In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.

A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.

FIG. 6 shows a third embodiment. The vibration device 10 carries one or more stirring elements 48. Because the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 while the bearing face 26 is of a low-friction material, the vibration device 10 is held down and at the same time free to move over the exposed face 38, unlike a device that is gripped at one place. Embodiment with stirring elements

FIG. 6 shows a third embodiment. The vibration device 10 carries one or more stirring elements 48. Because the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 while the bearing face 26 is of a low-friction material, the vibration device 10 is held down and at the same time free to move over the exposed face 38, unlike a device that is gripped at one place. The vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 acts through the stirring elements 48 to produce a constant forward motion of the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38. The vibration device 10 therefore advances from area to area of the covering element 36 without tension being applied to a flexible pulling element 46 and without being guided by hand, while the pressure differential is maintained throughout. The stirring elements 48 are shown schematically in FIG. 6.

In this embodiment the operator supplies neither the force that holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 nor the force that moves it across the exposed face 38. The first is supplied by the pressure differential and the second by the vibration of the vibration device 10 acting through the stirring elements 48, so the vibration that is being delivered into the covering element 36 also carries the vibration device 10 over it.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44, or by the vibration acting through the stirring elements 48 to advance the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38.

lines: Embodiment with stirring elements

-FIG. 6 shows a third embodiment. The vibration device 10 carries one or more stirring elements 48. Because the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 while the bearing face 26 is of a low-friction material, the vibration device 10 is held down and at the same time free to move over the exposed face 38, unlike a device that is gripped at one place. The vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 acts through the stirring elements 48 to produce a constant forward motion of the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38. The vibration device 10 therefore advances from area to area of the covering element 36 without tension being applied to a flexible pulling element 46 and without being guided by hand, while the pressure differential is maintained throughout. The stirring elements 48 are shown schematically in FIG. 6.

+FIG. 6 shows a third embodiment. The vibration device 10 carries one or more stirring elements 48. Because the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 while the bearing face 26 is of a low-friction material, the vibration device 10 is held down and at the same time free to move over the exposed face 38, unlike a device that is gripped at one place. The vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 acts through the stirring elements 48 to produce a constant forward motion of the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38. The vibration device 10 therefore advances from area to area of the covering element 36 without tension being applied to a flexible pulling element 46 and without being guided by hand, while the pressure differential is maintained throughout. The hold is not loosened to permit that motion: the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and the pressure differential continues to press the bearing face 26 onto the exposed face 38 while the vibration device 10 advances, so the vibration coupling into the covering element 36 is not interrupted by the movement. The stirring elements 48 are shown schematically in FIG. 6.

In this embodiment the operator supplies neither the force that holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 nor the force that moves it across the exposed face 38. The first is supplied by the pressure differential and the second by the vibration of the vibration device 10 acting through the stirring elements 48, so the vibration that is being delivered into the covering element 36 also carries the vibration device 10 over it.

input.summary: Added the autonomous mode the request supplies. The device now has a third disclosed embodiment: one or more stirring elements 48 carried by the vibration device, through which vibration from the vibration motor produces a constant forward motion over the exposed face, so the device advances from area to area without being pulled or guided. The field now covers devices advanced across the work by their own vibration; the Summary gains the embodiment and the reason it works, that the pressure differential holds the device down while the rigid low-friction bearing face leaves it free to move; the detailed description gains a section "Embodiment with stirring elements" plus a new option in the method of use; numerals.md gains 48; the Brief Description gains FIG. 6, and figures/FIG-6-THIRD-EMBODIMENT-WITH-STIRRING-ELEMENTS.md is a new sheet carrying 10, 24, 36 and 48. Claim 10 is a new device dependent on the stirring elements and claim 20 a new method dependent, with the system and method claims renumbered to 11 to 14 and 15 to 19 and every internal dependency updated, giving 20 claims and 3 independents. The previous review reported a pass with no findings, so nothing was changed for it.
reasoning: The request is new inventor disclosure, so it is authority. I took from it only what it states: small stirring elements, carried by the device, with the vibration causing a constant forward motion, and the reason it is possible, that the vacuum already holds the device while it stays free to move. I invented no form, count, size, material, angle or mounting location for the stirring elements, and the claims and description say only one or more of them, carried by the device.

I kept the inventor's own word, stirring element, as the element name rather than substituting a term of my own, and defined it functionally through what it does with the vibration. That keeps the text traceable to the passage that supports it.

I put the maintained hold into the new section deliberately: the hold is not loosened to permit the motion, the extraction keeps running and the differential keeps pressing the bearing face onto the tile while the device advances. That sentence is the technical explanation a later argument needs, because the closest art on vibration-driven travel, US-4934475-A, moves its body by using vibration to reduce the suction-adhering force. Here the coupling is never given up, which is the opposite relationship.

For the claims I made the stirring elements a dependent of claim 1 rather than a fourth independent claim. The autonomous mode only works because of what claim 1 already recites, the non-sealing rigid perimeter with continuous ingress, the sustained sub-atmospheric chamber and the low-friction bearing face that slides while held, so a standalone independent would either repeat all of that or claim something the disclosure does not support. Claim 10 also recites while the pressure differential is maintained, which is what separates it from vibration-driven travel that releases its hold.

I inserted the new device claim as claim 10 and renumbered rather than appending at the end, so the device, system and method groups stay contiguous and each dependent still follows its parent. I updated every internal reference: the system dependents now read claim 11 and the method dependents claim 15. The set is 20 claims with 3 independents, which stays inside the fee-free 20 and 3.

A new sheet was necessary rather than optional, because the drawings must show a feature that the claims recite. FIG. 6 follows the FIG. 5 pattern for the same machine so the two embodiment sheets read as the same device, and the stirring elements appear as two small blocks whose number, form and placement the brief expressly declares a per-sheet depiction convention, since the source gives none. That convention stays inside the figure brief; the application text asserts no location or shape for them.
The abstract was left alone. It is already near the 150 word limit, and the embodiment it would summarise is fully covered in the Summary and the detailed description.

The review returned a pass with no findings, and its two notes were about stale prose in the evidence file and unavailable pixel tooling rather than the draft, so there was nothing to repair. The five existing figure briefs and sheets were not touched, so only the new sheet needs rendering.

input.prior_art_strategy: Claim 1 is unchanged and still carries the combination clear of the art: a rigid low-friction perimeter member at the perimeter of the second side ending in a bearing face that leaves a clearance admitting ambient air continuously, an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric rate holds the chamber below atmospheric against that ingress, an all-rigid transmission path with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed, and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. The new stirring-element claims are dependent, so they inherit all of that, and the feature that keeps them clear of the closest reference is expressly recited: the device advances while the pressure differential is maintained. US-4934475-A is the only file that couples vibration to travel, and it does the opposite, using vibration to impart a lifting force that reduces the suction-adhering hold so the body can be driven along; the specification now states in its own words that here the hold is not loosened, the extraction keeps running and the coupling is not interrupted by the movement. US-10001245-B2 likewise gives up vacuum coupling to move, switching its generator to a blower mode and floating on an air cushion. DE-202021002652-U1 and US-11408462-B2 remain distinguished by their compliant holding walls, a rubber-elastic apron and elastic partitions, and US-11247858-B2 remains lifting and cleaning equipment that delivers no vibration into a laid covering element.
input.answer: The autonomous mode is in the application. The field now speaks of devices guided by hand, drawn by a flexible pulling element, or advanced across the work by their own vibration. The Summary adds the further embodiment in which the device carries one or more stirring elements and its own vibration acts through them to produce a constant forward motion over the exposed face, together with the reason it is possible: the pressure differential holds the device down while the rigid low-friction bearing face leaves it free to move. The detailed description has a new section, Embodiment with stirring elements, introducing the stirring elements 48 and stating that the device advances from area to area without tension on a flexible pulling element 46 and without being guided by hand, that the operator supplies neither the holding force nor the moving force, and that the hold is not loosened to permit the motion, the air-extraction mechanism 20 continuing to run and the differential continuing to press the bearing face 26 onto the exposed face 38 while the device advances. The method of use now offers that as a third way of translating the device. On the claims, claim 10 is a new device claim on the stirring elements and claim 20 a new method claim on advancing by them; the system claims are renumbered 11 to 14 and the method claims 15 to 19, with every internal dependency updated, leaving 20 claims and 3 independents. Because the claims recite the stirring elements, they had to be shown, so figures/FIG-6-THIRD-EMBODIMENT-WITH-STIRRING-ELEMENTS.md is added, carrying numerals 10, 24, 36 and 48, and the Brief Description of the Drawings gains a matching FIG. 6 sentence. Since your message gives no form, count or position for the stirring elements, none appears in the text: the sheet shows them as two small blocks and the brief expressly calls their number, form and placement a depiction convention for that sheet only. The previous review returned a pass with no findings, so nothing was changed on its account; its two notes concerned stale prose in the evidence file and unavailable pixel tooling rather than the draft, and the five existing sheets were left untouched.

3	Ledger result: the application text is almost entirely traceable. Every claim limitation in claims 1-20 traces to affirmative inventor passages: rigid base with first/second sides, motor on the first side, air-extraction mechanism (vacuum pump) on the first side in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side, rigid low-friction perimeter loop/skirt of plastic, metal, PTFE or a combination of rigid materials, non-sealing perimeter with continuous ambient ingress, extraction sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric, holding force replacing operator pressure, an all-rigid transmission path with no compliant member, sliding while held, handles for guiding, and the rope/wire/cable pulling element with decoupled control (disclosure lines 11-17). The stirring-element embodiment (summary para. 5, description "Embodiment with stirring elements", claims 10 and 20, FIG. 6, numeral 48, and the Field's "advanced across the work by their own vibration") traces to the final USER passage: "we can add small stirring elements and let the vibrations cause a constant forward motion ... we don't even need to pull or move it with the hand". Numeral integrity is clean: all 17 numerals in numerals.md appear in the description, none is used for two parts, no numeral appears in the text that is missing from the table, and the union of the six figure briefs' numeral lists equals the table exactly (10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42, 44, 46, 48). Each sheet carries at most seven unique numerals. Claim/description terminology is uniform ("air-extraction mechanism", "perimeter member", "bearing face", "clearance", "covering element", "exposed face"), and the claim relationships (chamber bounded by second side, perimeter member and exposed face; clearance along at least part; extraction rate sufficient while ingress continues; rigid path; slidable while the differential is maintained) are stated identically in the Summary, the Detailed Description and the claims. Twenty claims in three independent classes, and the Background's prior-art characterizations are outside this review. No drafting note, placeholder, bracketed request, open question, unresolved alternative, or human-directed instruction remains in any of the ten sections; the figure briefs contain only renderer geometry, and each generic form (rectangular slab, band, ring, column, blocks) is expressly confined to its own brief with the matching "shown schematically" recital in the Brief Description of the Drawings, with the application text left shape-neutral and free of any "by way of example" or "any closed outline" broadening. Two defects were verified. First, FIG. 6 draws the stirring elements 48 standing "on the top face of the body", which asserts a mounting on the first side of the base, remote from the work, a location the inventor never gave and which sits awkwardly against the described function of driving the device forward over the exposed face; the brief's own "placement ... is a depiction convention" disclaimer cannot carry a relationship of that kind. Second, FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 are sectional views whose cutting planes are identified only in prose ("taken through the base, the chamber and the perimeter member"; "taken at a place along the perimeter member where the clearance is present"): no view carries a designated section line, so no repeated designation exists in the source view, the figure brief and the drawing description. Everything else in the ledger is supported and internally consistent.

11	## Reviewer findings
12	
13	- **[critical] FIG. 6 mounts the stirring elements on the top face of the body, a location no inventor passage gives** (figures/FIG-6-THIRD-EMBODIMENT-WITH-STIRRING-ELEMENTS.md, "Geometry to be drawn", the paragraph beginning "Two small clo) - The figure brief places the stirring elements 48 on the upper face of the machine body, i.e. on the first side 14 of the base 12, facing away from the covering element 36. The only inventor statement about stirring elements is "we can add small stirring elements and let the vibrations cause a constant forward motion"; it gives no mounting face, no position relative to the base or the perimeter member, and no relationship to the work surface. A mounting face is not a mere outline or page placement: it fixes where the elements sit relative to the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the covering element 36, and a top-face mounting implies the elements stand clear of the work, which conveys technical substance and sits against the described function that "the vibration ... acts through the stirring elements 48 to produce a constant forward motion of the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38" (draft/08-detailed-description.md). The brief's disclaimer that "their number, form and placement on the body are a depiction convention for this sheet only" does not cure it, because the drawn geometry still asserts the relationship. The plural depiction itself is fine (the source says "stirring elements"), and the application text is correctly location-neutral ("The vibration device 10 carries one or more stirring elements 48"; claim 10 "one or more stirring elements carried by the vibration device") - the unsupported matter exists only in the figure brief.
14	  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-6-THIRD-EMBODIMENT-WITH-STIRRING-ELEMENTS.md replace the paragraph with: "Two small closed blocks, the stirring elements 48, are drawn carried by the machine against the front face of the rectangular body, each drawn broad enough for a point to stand well inside its front face. They are shown schematically; their number, form and drawn place are a depiction convention for this sheet only, no mounting face, no position relative to the base 12 or the perimeter member 24, and no engagement with the covering element 36 being asserted." Replace the labelling line with: "The stirring elements 48 are those two small blocks carried by the machine. Identified well inside the front face of the left-hand block." # FIG. 3 - Bottom plan view of the vibration device

**View:** Plan view looking straight up at the underside of the machine, nothing beneath the machine being drawn. Outline line work only, with no lettering drawn.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet shows the underside of the machine as a rectangular ring in the manner of a picture frame. Two closed rectangular outlines appear in the view, one held within the other: the outer edge of the ring and the inner edge of the ring. The rectangular plan form is a depiction convention for this sheet only, both parts being shown schematically.

The perimeter member 24 is the ring surface. It runs continuously from the outer edge across to the inner edge, presenting one plain surface across its whole breadth, and it runs all the way round the four sides, carrying round each corner without interruption, so that it reads as one closed loop. It is broad along each of its four sides, broad enough for a point standing well inside it to be clear of both the outer edge and the inner edge; its breadth is schematic and no proportion is asserted.

The second side 16 is the face at which this view looks straight, and it appears as the area held within the inner edge of the ring. That area is one plain face, bounded on all four sides by the inner edge alone and running continuously from the inner edge on one side across to the inner edge on the opposite side. It is broad enough for a point standing well inside it to be clear of the inner edge all round.

Beyond the outer edge lies the surrounding background. The whole ring stands well inside the drawing area and is drawn large within it.

Two broken cutting-plane lines are drawn across the view, each carrying an arrow at each of its two ends and the same designation repeated at both ends, so that one reads as line 2-2 and the other as line 4-4.

The line 2-2 runs horizontally. It begins in the background just outside the left-hand side of the ring, crosses the ring surface on the left, the enclosed face and the ring surface on the right, and ends in the background just outside the right-hand side of the ring. Both of its arrows point toward the lower limit of the drawing area.

The line 4-4 runs vertically. It begins in the background just outside the upper side of the ring, crosses the ring surface there, the enclosed face and the ring surface on the lower side, and ends in the background just outside the lower side of the ring. Both of its arrows point toward the left-hand limit of the drawing area.

- The perimeter member 24 is the ring surface lying between the outer edge and the inner edge. Identified well inside that surface along the left-hand side of the ring, clear of both edges.
- The second side 16 is the plain face held within the inner edge. Identified well inside that face, clear of the inner edge all round.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 16, 24

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 16
- 24

# FIG. 2 - Vertical section through the chamber

**View:** Vertical section through the vibration device of FIG. 1 and the covering element 36 beneath it. Line work with hatching on cut material, and no lettering drawn. The vibration motor and the handle are omitted, and the clearance appears only in FIG. 4.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet shows four bodies, all shown schematically, and one broken line: one horizontal hatched slab, the base 12; one closed loop cut twice, appearing as two short hatched legs hanging from the underside of the slab, one at each end of the slab, the outer side of each leg flush with that end so that the loop runs at the perimeter of the underside; one hatched band across the bottom, the covering element 36, on which both legs stand; and one closed housing standing on the upper face of the slab, the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The slab, the two legs and the band are the cut bodies. The slab is filled with regularly spaced parallel hatching rising to the right at about 45 degrees, both legs are filled with such hatching falling to the right at about 45 degrees, and the band is filled with such hatching rising to the right at about 75 degrees. The housing lies outside the cut and is drawn in plain outline, its interior left as open paper.

The slab is drawn thick, and its upper face is visible on each side of the housing. The lower end of each leg rests on the band.

One broken line runs from inside the housing to the chamber 22, indicating schematically the fluid communication between the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the chamber 22. That line stops at the upper face of the base 12 and resumes below its lower face, no passage through the base 12 being drawn or asserted.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The base 12 is the horizontal hatched slab. Identified well inside its hatching.
- The first side 14 is the upper face of the base 12, seen edge on as the upper edge line of the slab. Identified at that upper edge line where it runs clear of the housing, a point touching that line from either side counting as on it.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is the unhatched housing on the slab. Identified well inside that housing.
- The chamber 22 is the broad open space between the two legs, below the base 12 and above the band. Identified well inside that open space.
- The perimeter member 24 is the closed loop hanging from the base 12, cut twice so that it appears as the two hatched legs. Identified well inside the hatching of the right-hand leg.
- The covering element 36 is the hatched band across the bottom. Identified well inside its hatching.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 12, 14, 20, 22, 24, 36
