FIG. 2: the hatching is respecified stroke by stroke rather than by angle alone, each stroke of the slab starting low on the left and ending high on the right like a forward slash, each stroke of both legs starting high on the left and ending low on the right like a backslash so a leg's strokes cross the slab's where they meet, and each stroke of the band steep and close to upright, much nearer to vertical than the legs' strokes. FIG. 6: the band's front strip must now be deep enough at every point across its width to hold a point clear of both edges, and numeral 24 targets well inside the right-hand part of that strip. To hold FIG. 2 within the length limit I compressed eight phrases that repeated wording already in the brief; it is at 2793 characters and every brief is at or below the limit. No claim, numeral definition, drawing description or disclosed embodiment changed.
reasoning: FIG. 1's endpoint failed because the target was a line rather than an area: on a perspective slab the left-hand upright outline meets the top face edge at a corner, so a dot placed along it can land on the vertex. The cure is to give numeral 10 an interior region, and the sheet already presents the slab's left-hand end to the viewer, so naming that end as a four-sided face and drawing it broad enough to hold a point makes the target unambiguous without adding structure. Numeral 12 still takes the front face, so the two remain distinct.

FIG. 2 has now failed on hatch direction through several formulations that specified degrees. Degrees are evidently not what the renderer follows, so I described the strokes themselves: where each stroke begins and ends, with the familiar forward slash and backslash shapes, and the band as steep and close to upright. I also stated the consequence a reviewer looks for, that a leg's strokes cross the slab's where the two meet, which is a positive geometric relationship rather than a rendering prohibition.

Hatch direction is a sectioning convention and carries no technical content, so nothing about the invention moved: the four bodies, the flush legs at the perimeter of the underside, the legs standing on the band, and the broken indicating line that stops at the base faces without asserting a passage are all unchanged.

FIG. 6's numeral 24 sat in a rejected coordinate cluster, which usually means the target region is too shallow to hold a dot reliably. I fixed the cause rather than the coordinate: the front strip of the band must now be deep enough at every point across its width for a point to stand well inside it clear of both edges, and the numeral targets the right-hand part of that strip, away from the blocks the sheet also carries. Right-hand is a stable direction, not an ordinal that could be read either way.
I kept every target broad and removed the old FIG. 6 wording that located the dot by reference to two bounding lines, which is the kind of narrow instruction that produces borderline placements.

The rewritten FIG. 2 brief ran long, so I compressed phrases that repeat what other sentences already carry. Nothing load-bearing was dropped: all four bodies, the hatching assignment, the contacts, the fluid-communication line and all six numeral entries with their tolerance wording remain.
No text file was touched. The failures are all drawing-side, and the application text, claims, numeral table and drawing descriptions already match the six-figure plan restored in the previous turn.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged. Claim 1 rests on the rigid low-friction perimeter member at the perimeter of the second side, ending in a bearing face that leaves a clearance admitting ambient air continuously; an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric rate holds the chamber below atmospheric against that ingress; an all-rigid transmission path with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. The FIG. 2 repair matters to that position: hatching that distinguishes the base from the perimeter member and the perimeter member from the covering element keeps the section reading as two rigid parts rigidly connected and bearing on the tile, which is what separates the invention from the rubber-elastic apron of DE-202021002652-U1 and the elastic partitions of US-11408462-B2. Claims 10 and 20 remain dependent and keep the recital that the device advances while the differential is maintained, distinguishing US-4934475-A, whose vibration reduces the suction-adhering hold to permit travel, and US-10001245-B2, which floats on a blower-fed air cushion to move. US-11247858-B2 remains lifting and cleaning equipment that delivers no vibration into a laid covering element.
input.answer: All three sheets are repaired in their briefs, with no change to the text. On FIG. 1 the trouble was that numeral 10 was aimed at a line, the slab's left-hand upright outline, which meets the top face edge at a corner where a dot can land ambiguously. On FIG. 2 the hatching had been specified by angle and the renderer kept drawing all three cut bodies alike, so the strokes are now described directly: in the slab each stroke starts low on the left and ends high on the right, like a forward slash; in both legs each stroke starts high on the left and ends low on the right, like a backslash, so a leg's strokes cross the slab's where they meet; and in the band each stroke is steep, close to upright and leaning slightly to the right, much nearer to vertical than the legs' strokes. That is a sectioning convention only, so the bodies, the flush legs at the perimeter of the underside, the legs standing on the band and the broken indicating line that stops at the base faces are unchanged. On FIG. 6 numeral 24 sat in a rejected cluster because the band's front strip gave it too little room, so the strip must now be deep enough at every point across its width for a point to stand well inside it clear of both edges, and the numeral targets the right-hand part of that strip, away from the blocks. Rewriting FIG. 2 ran the brief long, so I compressed eight phrases that repeated wording already present; it stands at 2793 characters and every brief is at or below the limit, with all bodies, contacts, endpoints and numeral lists intact.

disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile seen in perspective, as in FIG. 1, filling the lower part of the drawing area. The machine stands on its left-hand part, with open tile to the right.

The machine and the tile are shown schematically, the machine as one plain rectangular body standing on a band that runs round its underside, the band alone touching the tile, these forms being a convention for this sheet only.

The band meets the underside of the body and follows the same rectangular run, its front surface facing the viewer as one unbroken strip across the whole width and drawn deep, a broad clear surface standing between the underside of the body above and the tile below, deep enough at every point across its width for a point to stand well inside it clear of both edges; its depth is schematic. It stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting the tile.

The rectangular body is drawn broad and tall, its front face turned toward the viewer as a large plain surface. Its left-hand end is one long straight edge between the top face and the band.

Two small closed blocks, each a stirring element 48, are drawn carried by the machine against the front face of the rectangular body, each drawn broad enough for a point to stand well inside its front face. They are shown schematically; their number, form and drawn place are a depiction convention for this sheet only, no mounting face, no position relative to the body or the perimeter member 24, and no engagement with the covering element 36 being asserted.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine standing on the covering element 36, the rectangular body with its band and the blocks it carries. Identified on the outer boundary line of the machine at the left-hand end of the rectangular body, anywhere along that long straight edge.

- The covering element 36 is that large plain tile, on which the machine stands. Identified well inside the open stretch of tile to the right of the machine.
- Each of the two small blocks carried by the machine is a stirring element 48. Identified well inside the front face of the left-hand block.

SOURCE LEDGER - clean on disclosure fidelity. Every technical element in the proposed text traces to an affirmative inventor passage:

• Rigid base 12 with first side 14 / second side 16, vibration motor 18 on the first side, air-extraction mechanism 20 (vacuum pump) on the first side in fluid communication with chamber 22 on the second side → "providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base."
• Perimeter member 24 as a rigid closed loop/skirt at the perimeter of the second side, of plastic, metal, PTFE or a combination of rigid materials, terminating in bearing face 26 → "The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials."
• Not a seal, free of rubber/elastomer/foam, rigid contact, clearance 34 admitting ambient air continuously, extraction rate sufficient to hold the chamber below atmospheric under continuous ingress, resulting pressure differential holding the device without operator downward force → "the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam… restricts airflow into the chamber… continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward."
• All-rigid vibration transmission path with no elastomeric/foam/resilient mount interposed, and less damping than a flexible suction cup → "Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup"; damper/damping-handle contrast → "Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles… also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile."
• Slidability while held → "the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact."
• Handle 44 for guiding (claims 8, 18) → "one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface."
• Flexible pulling element 46 (rope, wire, cable), system claims 11–14 and decoupled control → "a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device… decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling."
• Stirring elements 48, constant forward motion, autonomous advance without pulling or hand guidance (summary ¶5, description "Embodiment with stirring elements", claims 10 and 20, FIG. 6, Field) → USER: "the device is already connected via vaccum and unlike other machines it is free to move, so we don't even need to pull or move it with the hand, we can add small stirring elements and let the vibrations cause a constant forward motion."

1. A vibration device for bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the vibration device comprising:

a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side;

a vibration motor coupled to the first side;

a perimeter member extending from the second side at a perimeter thereof and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, the perimeter member being rigid and of a low-friction material and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face that is an end face of the perimeter member, the chamber being bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and, when the bearing face is placed against an exposed face of the covering element, by the exposed face, and a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber; and

an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber, the air-extraction mechanism being operable to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while the ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, a resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device against the covering element;

wherein a vibration transmission path from the vibration motor to the bearing face passes through the base and the perimeter member, each member of the vibration transmission path is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

wherein the bearing face is slidable over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained.

2. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the perimeter member is a closed loop that runs around the chamber, the closed loop restricting a flow of the ambient air into the chamber through the clearance without closing the clearance and without forming a complete airtight seal.

3. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the low-friction material of the perimeter member is plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

4. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the perimeter member is free of rubber, elastomer and foam, and makes rigid contact with the exposed face.

5. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the pressure differential produces a holding force sufficient to hold the vibration device against the exposed face without a downward force being applied by an operator.

6. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the air-extraction mechanism is operable to withdraw air from the chamber continuously while the vibration device is in use.

7. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the air-extraction mechanism is a vacuum pump.

8. The vibration device of claim 1, further comprising a handle arranged to guide the vibration device over the exposed face while the pressure differential holds the vibration device against the covering element.

9. The vibration device of claim 1, further comprising a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device, the vibration device being translatable over the exposed face by tension applied to the flexible pulling element while the pressure differential is maintained.

10. The vibration device of claim 1, further comprising one or more stirring elements carried by the vibration device, wherein vibration from the vibration motor acts through the one or more stirring elements to produce a forward motion of the vibration device over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained.

11. A system for bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the system comprising:

a vibration device comprising a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side, a vibration motor coupled to the first side, a perimeter member extending from the second side at a perimeter thereof and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, and an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber,

the perimeter member being rigid and of a low-friction material and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face that is an end face of the perimeter member, the chamber being bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and, when the bearing face is placed against an exposed face of the covering element, by the exposed face, and a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber,

the air-extraction mechanism being operable to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while the ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, a resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device against the covering element,

wherein a vibration transmission path from the vibration motor to the bearing face passes through the base and the perimeter member, each member of the vibration transmission path is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device, the flexible pulling element being arranged to move the vibration device across the exposed face when tension is applied to it,

whereby a position of the vibration device over the exposed face is controlled by tension applied to the flexible pulling element while a force holding the vibration device against the covering element is supplied independently of the flexible pulling element by the pressure differential.

12. The system of claim 11, wherein the flexible pulling element is a rope, a wire or a cable.

13. The system of claim 11, wherein the low-friction material of the perimeter member is plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

14. The system of claim 11, wherein the perimeter member is free of rubber, elastomer and foam, and wherein the pressure differential produces a holding force sufficient to hold the vibration device against the exposed face without a downward force being applied by an operator.

15. A method of bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the method comprising:

placing a vibration device on an exposed face of the covering element that has been laid on the bonding material, the vibration device comprising a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side, a vibration motor coupled to the first side, a rigid perimeter member of a low-friction material extending from the second side at a perimeter thereof and surrounding a chamber located on the second side and terminating in a bearing face that is an end face of the perimeter member, and an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber, whereby the bearing face is brought against the exposed face so that the chamber is bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and the exposed face, with a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber;

operating the air-extraction mechanism to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, and holding the vibration device against the covering element by a resulting pressure differential;

operating the vibration motor and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor to the covering element along a vibration transmission path passing through the base and the perimeter member to the bearing face, each member of the vibration transmission path being rigid and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount being interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

translating the vibration device across the exposed face, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face over the exposed face, so that the vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element.

16. The method of claim 15, wherein the pressure differential is maintained continuously while the vibration device is translated across the exposed face, so that the vibration device is held against the covering element and slid over the exposed face at the same time.

17. The method of claim 15, wherein the vibration device is translated across the exposed face by applying tension to a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device.

18. The method of claim 15, wherein the vibration device is translated across the exposed face by guiding the vibration device with a handle, and wherein the pressure differential holds the vibration device against the covering element without a downward force being required from an operator.

19. The method of claim 15, wherein the low-friction material of the perimeter member is polytetrafluoroethylene.

20. The method of claim 15, wherein the translating is done by vibration from the vibration motor acting through one or more stirring elements carried by the vibration device to advance the vibration device over the exposed face, without tension being applied to a flexible pulling element and without the vibration device being guided by hand.

The machine is one plain rectangular slab, the base 12, standing on a band that runs round its underside. Three closed blocks stand side by side on the top face of the slab: the left-hand block is the vibration motor 18, the middle block is the handle 44, and the right-hand block is the air-extraction mechanism 20. lines: The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

-Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

input.summary: All three findings are fixed. Section designations now exist and match: the FIG. 3 brief draws two broken section lines, each beginning and ending in the background just beyond the outer edge of the ring, each crossing the ring surface and the face within it, each carrying an arrow at both ends and its designation at both ends; one runs horizontally with both arrows toward the lower part of the sheet, marked 2-2, crossing the ring where the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element, and the other runs vertically with both arrows toward the left-hand part, marked 4-4, crossing where the clearance is present. Its View statement permits those designations as the only lettering. The same designations appear in the FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 brief View lines, in the Brief Description entries for FIG. 2 and FIG. 4, and in the detailed description. FIG. 1's numeral 10 is back on the outer boundary line, along the left-hand outer edge of the silhouette formed by the slab and the band together, clear of the front face and of the blocks, matching the convention used on FIG. 5 and FIG. 6, and the geometry sentence now describes that continuous outer boundary rather than an end face. Claim 15 now recites a second side opposite the first side and a perimeter member terminating, remote from the base, in the bearing face, matching claims 1 and 11 and the description. Compressions in FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 keep every brief at or below 2800 characters.
reasoning: The designation chain had to exist in three places at once, so I wrote it in all of them in one pass: the source-view brief draws and marks both lines, both resulting-view briefs name the line they are taken on, and the Brief Description and detailed description use the same phrase. A designation named in only one of those places is what left the earlier attempts unmatched.

The FIG. 3 lines are specified as drawing geometry rather than as bare labels: each has its start and end in the background beyond the ring, its alignment, the viewing direction of both arrows, and its designation repeated at both ends, and the brief states expressly that the lines are drawing conventions asserting no dimension or proportion. The View statement had to permit lettering again, limited to those designations, since a sheet cannot both print 2-2 and 4-4 and carry no lettering.

Placing 2-2 where the perimeter member bears on the covering element and 4-4 where the clearance is present matches what the text already says about the two planes, so the lines record a distinction the specification makes rather than introducing one.

On FIG. 1 I reverted my previous change. Moving numeral 10 inside the slab's left-hand end face cured a corner-vertex placement but created a worse problem, two numerals terminating inside surfaces of the same slab, so a reader could not tell which meant the assembly and which the base. The outer-boundary target is what FIG. 5 and FIG. 6 already use for numeral 10, and specifying that the slab and band present one continuous outer boundary on that side gives the leader a long edge to land on rather than a corner.

Claim 15 was the only independent claim missing the two relationships that claims 1 and 11 and the description use for the same parts. Adding opposite the first side and remote from the base removes the literal reading in which the sides are not opposed and the bearing face could be at either end, and it costs no scope that the description supports.

Both additions pushed briefs over the length limit, so I compressed wording that repeated what other sentences already carry, in FIG. 3 the four-sides restatements and in FIG. 2 three short phrases. Every body, contact, hatching assignment, section line and numeral endpoint survives, and all six briefs are at or below 2800 characters.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged. Claim 1 rests on the rigid low-friction perimeter member at the perimeter of the second side, ending in a bearing face that leaves a clearance admitting ambient air continuously; an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric rate holds the chamber below atmospheric against that ingress; an all-rigid transmission path with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. Claim 15 now states the same base and perimeter-member relationships as claims 1 and 11, so the method claim cannot be read more loosely than the apparatus it performs. The two designated planes carry the distinction the argument depends on into the drawings, line 2-2 where the perimeter member bears rigidly on the covering element and line 4-4 where the clearance admits air, which is the non-sealing rigid perimeter that separates the invention from the rubber-elastic apron of DE-202021002652-U1 and the elastic partitions of US-11408462-B2. Claims 10 and 20 remain dependent and keep the recital that the device advances while the differential is maintained, distinguishing US-4934475-A, whose vibration reduces the suction-adhering hold to permit travel, and US-10001245-B2, which floats on a blower-fed air cushion to move. US-11247858-B2 remains lifting and cleaning equipment that delivers no vibration into a laid covering element.

reasoning: The same numeral failed on the same part on two sheets while passing on FIG. 5, which shows the identical machine from the same viewpoint. They now stand against the upper part of the front face, clear above the band. That is a per-sheet depiction convention, and the brief still declares that no mounting face or position relative to the body or the perimeter member 24 is asserted, so the invention is untouched.

I did not move numeral 24 off either sheet. Dropping it would have satisfied the check while removing the label from the very part the claims turn on, and it would have forced the perimeter member out of both figure descriptions.

Because the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 while the bearing face 26 is of a low-friction material, the vibration device 10 is held down and at the same time free to move over the exposed face 38, unlike a device that is gripped at one place. 2	
3	The application text traces cleanly to the inventor's sources. Every claim limitation, numbered part and described relationship (rigid base, motor on the first side, air-extraction mechanism in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side, rigid low-friction perimeter loop terminating in a bearing face, the non-sealing clearance and continuous ingress, the sustained sub-atmospheric chamber and holding force, the all-rigid transmission path, sliding while held, handles, the rope/wire/cable pulling element with decoupled control, and the stirring elements added in the later inventor message) is supported by an exact passage in input/disclosure.md or input/conversation.md, and the drawing sheets add no structure the text does not already state (the base slab, blocks, housing, bands and loops are expressly declared schematic conventions, and the text stays neutral about their form and placement). All four [REF:...] characterisations in the Background match their prior_art/ files, including the negative statements about US-11247858-B2. Terminology is consistent between claims, description, numeral table and briefs, numerals 10-48 each label one part everywhere, and each cited figure shows what the text says it shows. Two drawing defects remain, both in the rendered sheets rather than in the specification: leader terminals colliding with the cutting-plane lines in FIG. 3, and stirring-element placement in FIG. 6 that contradicts its own brief. Neither creates unsupported matter, and both have automatic fixes in the existing figure briefs.
4	
5	## Reviewer findings
6	
7	- **[major] In FIG. 3 both leader terminal dots land on cutting-plane line 2-2, and numeral 16 lands exactly on the 2-2/4-4 crossing** (figures/rendered-FIG-3.png; figures/FIG-3-BOTTOM-PLAN-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE.md (callout list and section-line par) - On the composited sheet the terminal dot of numeral 16 sits at the exact centre of the view, where the broken horizontal cutting-plane line (2-2) and the broken vertical cutting-plane line (4-4) cross; the leader from '16' runs down-right and stops on that crossing, so on the printed sheet numeral 16 reads as designating the cutting-plane lines rather than the plain face inside the inner edge of the ring. The dot of numeral 24 lies on the same horizontal 2-2 line: it is at the line's height in the left-hand band of the ring, with the dashes visibly continuing at that height on both sides of it. This does not conflict with any check that was actually run. The recorded endpoint evidence was taken in the 1400x900 raw-geometry frame, whose companion geometry review states of the section lines that they are 'excluded from this review per instructions; no such paths are drawn', i.e. the frame the dots were certified in contains no cutting-plane lines; and the section marks were located by a separate reviewer that placed both lines through the centre of the figure ('The horizontal line is placed at the vertical midpoint (y=500), and the vertical line is placed at the horizontal midpoint (x=500)'), the same centre at which numeral 16's dot was placed. So the two records are each internally correct but were never compared, and the collision appears only in the final sheet. A section designation is not a reference numeral, and a numeral leader must not terminate on one.
8	  - Suggested fix: In the FIG. 3 brief, keep both section lines but take them off the mid-lines and keep the callouts clear of them: change the section-line paragraph to draw the horizontal 2-2 line across the lower part of the view and the vertical 4-4 line across the right-hand part, each still beginning and ending in the background just beyond the outer edge and still crossing the ring (arrow and designation instructions unchanged); and change the callout list to read 'The second side 16 ... Identified well inside that face in its upper right region, clear of both section lines.' and 'The perimeter member 24 ... Identified well inside that surface along the left-hand side of the ring, clear of both section lines.' Then re-render FIG. 3.
9	- **[minor] FIG. 6 draws the stirring elements at the bottom of the front face, against the band, not where its own brief places them** (figures/rendered-FIG-6.png; figures/FIG-6-THIRD-EMBODIMENT-WITH-STIRRING-ELEMENTS.md; review/figure-audit-evidence.json,) - The brief and the recorded geometry summary both say the two blocks are drawn against the upper part of the body's front face and clear above the band. On the sheet both blocks sit at the bottom of that face, immediately at the band: the left-hand block occupies roughly y 375-440 within a front face that spans roughly y 130-410 at that x, so its lower edge reaches the line where the body meets the band, and the right-hand block visibly straddles that junction line. My reading of the junction line carries about +/-20 px of uncertainty, but the left block's separation from the top edge of the face (about 245 px) is far outside that margin, so the 'upper part' instruction is plainly not met. Nothing unsupported is asserted by this: the specification says only that 'The vibration device 10 carries one or more stirring elements 48' and that they 'are shown schematically in FIG. 6', claim 10 and claim 20 are location-neutral, and the blocks do not touch the covering element 36. The defect is that the authoritative brief and the sheet disagree.
10	  - Suggested fix: Conform the brief to the sheet by replacing that sentence with: 'Two small closed blocks, each a stirring element 48, are drawn carried by the machine on the front face of the rectangular body, each drawn broad enough for a point to stand well inside its front face, and neither touching the tile.' (keeping the following convention sentence unchanged); alternatively keep the present wording and re-render FIG. 6 with both blocks wholly within the upper half of the front face, well above the line where the body meets the band.
11

# FIG. 3 - Bottom plan view of the vibration device

**View:** Plan view looking straight up at the underside of the machine, nothing beneath the machine being drawn. Outline line work only; the only lettering drawn is the numeral 2 at both ends of one section line and the numeral 4 at both ends of the other.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet shows the underside of the machine as a rectangular ring in the manner of a picture frame. Two closed rectangular outlines appear, one held within the other: the outer edge of the ring and the inner edge. The rectangular plan form is a depiction convention for this sheet only, both parts shown schematically.

The perimeter member 24 is the ring surface. It runs continuously from the outer edge across to the inner edge as one plain surface, and all the way round, carrying round each corner without interruption, so that it reads as one closed loop. It is broad enough along each side for a point well inside it to be clear of both edges.

The second side 16 is the face at which this view looks straight, appearing as the area held within the inner edge of the ring. That area is one plain face, bounded by the inner edge alone and continuous from that edge across to the opposite side. It is broad enough for a point well inside it to be clear of the inner edge.

Beyond the outer edge lies background. The whole ring stands well inside the drawing area, drawn large within it.

Two broken section lines are drawn across the view, one horizontal across the lower part of the view and one vertical across the right-hand part. Each begins and ends in the background just beyond the outer edge and crosses the ring surface and the face within it.

The horizontal line carries a short arrow at each of its two ends, both pointing toward the lower part of the sheet, and the numeral 2 at each of its two ends, so that it reads as section line 2-2 and leads to the sectional view of FIG. 2. It crosses the ring where the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element.

The vertical line carries a short arrow at each of its two ends, both pointing toward the left-hand part of the sheet, and the numeral 4 at each of its two ends, so that it reads as section line 4-4 and leads to the sectional view of FIG. 4. It crosses the ring where the clearance is present.

The section lines are drawing conventions and assert no proportion.

- The perimeter member 24 is the ring surface between the outer edge and the inner edge. Identified well inside that surface along the left-hand side of the ring, clear of both section lines.
- The second side 16 is the plain face held within the inner edge. Identified well inside that face in its upper left region, clear of both section lines.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 16, 24

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 16
- 24

input.summary: The request is the standing gate instruction, so the work is the two drawing findings. FIG. 3: the section lines are moved off the mid-lines, the horizontal 2-2 line now crossing the lower part of the view and the vertical 4-4 line the right-hand part, each still beginning and ending in the background just beyond the outer edge, still crossing the ring surface and the enclosed face, and still carrying an arrow and its designation numeral at both ends; the two callouts now require their terminal dots to stand clear of both section lines, numeral 24 along the left-hand side of the ring and numeral 16 in the upper left region of the enclosed face, which is the quadrant left open once 2-2 runs low and 4-4 runs right. FIG. 6: the sentence placing the stirring-element blocks on the upper part of the front face is replaced by the neutral instruction that the two blocks are drawn carried by the machine on the front face of the rectangular body, each broad enough to hold a point, and neither touching the tile, with the convention sentence that follows unchanged. Trims in FIG. 3 keep it at 2787 characters, and FIG. 6 stands at 2444. No claim, numeral definition, description passage or disclosed embodiment changed.
reasoning: The FIG. 3 collision is a real defect and the cure is geometric: while both cutting-plane lines ran through the centre of the view, the natural interior target for numeral 16 was exactly the crossing, so the leader read as designating the section marks rather than the second side. Moving 2-2 low and 4-4 right frees the interior without changing what either line means, and both keep their endpoints beyond the outer edge, their arrow directions and their designations at both ends.

I placed numeral 16 in the upper left region rather than the upper right named in the suggested wording, because with 4-4 crossing the right-hand part of the view the upper right is the quadrant that line now runs through; upper left is the region left clear by both lines. The instruction to stay clear of both section lines is stated explicitly for both callouts so the requirement does not depend on my choice of region.

For FIG. 6 I removed the placement instruction rather than defending it. That upper-part wording was a constraint I introduced myself, to stop the blocks crowding numeral 24 on the band, and numeral 24 is no longer on that sheet, so the constraint had lost its purpose and was an invented rendering control rather than disclosed geometry.

What replaces it keeps the only relationship that matters and is source-supported: the blocks are carried by the machine on the front face and neither touches the tile, which prevents them being read as engaging the covering element. The convention sentence following it still declares their number, form and drawn position a depiction convention for that sheet, so nothing about location enters the application.

The application text needed no change for either finding. It says only that the vibration device 10 carries one or more stirring elements 48 and that they are shown schematically in FIG. 6, and claims 10 and 20 stay location-neutral.

Adding the placement and clearance wording ran FIG. 3 long, so I compressed six phrases that repeated what other sentences already carry. The two-outline ring topology, the continuous loop through every corner, the enclosed face, both section lines with their arrows and designations, and both numeral targets all survive.

input.summary: The single finding is fixed in the FIG. 2 brief. The perimeter member is no longer directed to be drawn as two short legs; it now appears as two hatched legs hanging from the underside of the slab, one at each end and flush with it so the loop runs at the perimeter of the underside, each leg drawn deep enough for its hatching and a point well inside it to read clearly, its depth schematic as in FIG. 1. The word short is gone, so FIG. 2 no longer states a relative proportion for a member the inventor gave no dimension for, and the schematic qualifier now matches the one FIG. 1 already carries for the same part. Nothing else in the sheet changed: the four bodies, the flush placement at the perimeter, the hatching assignment, the legs resting on the band, the broken indicating line that stops at the base faces without asserting a passage, and all six numeral entries are as they were. Compressions elsewhere in the brief hold it at 2790 characters. No claim, numeral definition, description passage, drawing description or other figure brief was touched.
reasoning: FIG. 2 is expressly a section through the device of FIG. 1, so the two sheets must depict the same part at the same proportions. Directing that the legs be short while FIG. 1 requires the same member to be drawn deep with its edges well apart gave the renderer contradictory instructions for one part, and the shallow version also fixed the chamber depth by implication.

The inventor gives no dimension for the loop, only that the perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt of low-friction material, so the repair had to remove the proportion rather than pick one. What replaces it is a legibility requirement, deep enough for the hatching and an interior point to read, which is a depiction need rather than a statement about the part.

I carried FIG. 1's qualifier across verbatim in substance, its depth schematic as in FIG. 1, so both briefs now mark the drawn depth as a convention and neither can be read as asserting how deep the loop is.

The legibility wording also serves the endpoint for numeral 24 on this sheet, which targets well inside the hatching of the right-hand leg; a leg drawn too shallow is exactly the condition that produces a borderline dot, so the same sentence removes the inconsistency and protects the placement.

input.summary: The FIG. 2 hatching specification is rewritten. The brief no longer assigns a stroke direction to each cut body; it now states that the slab, the legs and the band are the cut bodies, each filled with regularly spaced parallel hatching, and that where two of them meet a plain solid line is drawn along the join, so the slab, each leg and the band each read as a separate body with its own hatched interior. The housing still lies outside the cut in plain outline with open paper inside. That removes the brief-to-pixel mismatch the review reported on all three bodies while keeping what the sheet has to show, three separate sectioned parts with the perimeter member standing between the base and the covering element. Nothing else on the sheet changed: the four bodies, the legs flush at each end so the loop runs at the perimeter of the underside, the legs resting on the band, the schematic leg depth, the broken indicating line that stops at the base faces without asserting a passage, and all six numeral entries are as they were. The brief is now 2637 characters. No claim, numeral definition, description passage, drawing description or other figure brief was touched.
reasoning: Hatch direction on this sheet has now been specified four ways, by degrees, by rising and falling, by forward slash and backslash with a crossing at the junction, and by stroke start and end points, and each time the render came back with one uniform forty-five degree pattern on all three bodies. The mismatch is between the brief and the pixels, and the direction of repair had to change because the geometry instruction was the part that could not be satisfied.

Hatch angle is a sectioning convention, not disclosed geometry. The inventor's sources say nothing about it, so removing the per-body assignment takes nothing out of the invention and removes an invented rendering constraint of exactly the kind that should be dropped rather than defended.

What the sheet actually needs is for the three sectioned parts to read as three parts, and I now require that positively and by something the renderer does draw: a plain solid line along each join, with each body carrying its own hatched interior. The base to leg junction and the leg to band contact are therefore still legible as boundaries between separate bodies.

I kept the hatching requirement itself, since the bodies are cut and must be shown as cut material, and kept the housing outside the cut in plain outline so the air-extraction mechanism remains distinguishable from the sectioned parts without relying on angle.
I left FIG. 4 alone. Its per-body angle assignments have passed recent inspections, only FIG. 2 was reported, and editing a sheet that renders correctly would risk it for nothing.
No application text refers to hatching, so nothing needed resynchronizing, and the shortened paragraph leaves the brief comfortably inside the length limit.

FIG. 2 still shows the perimeter member as a separate rigid body hanging from the base and bearing on the covering element, which is the relationship that separates the invention from the rubber-elastic apron of DE-202021002652-U1 and the elastic partitions of US-11408462-B2; that separateness now rests on drawn boundary lines rather than on hatch angle. US-11247858-B2 remains lifting and cleaning equipment that delivers no vibration into a laid covering element.

input.summary: The report names no sheet, so I hardened the two that changed most recently and are the plausible source of a geometry, leader or OCR failure. FIG. 2: the hatching requirement now states the relationship a section reviewer checks rather than an absolute angle the renderer has repeatedly ignored, namely that where two cut bodies meet a plain solid line is drawn along the join and the strokes of the two bodies cross that line at different slopes, so the slab, each leg and the band each read as a separate body with its own hatched interior. FIG. 3: both callouts now say where their dots must sit relative to the section lines, numeral 24 in the ring surface along the left-hand side above the horizontal line, and numeral 16 in the upper left region of the enclosed face above the horizontal line and to the left of the vertical one, clear of both, so no leader can terminate on a cutting-plane line. Compressions in FIG. 3 hold it at 2798 characters and FIG. 2 stands at 2708. No claim, numeral definition, description passage, drawing description or numeral list changed, and the other four briefs were left untouched.
reasoning: With the failing sheet unnamed, the useful evidence is which briefs changed since the last render. FIG. 2's hatching paragraph and FIG. 3's section-line placement were both rewritten in the last two turns, so those are the two sheets whose pixels are newest and least proven.

On FIG. 2 I did not restore per-body angles. Specifying degrees, then rising and falling, then slash shapes, then stroke start and end points all failed against the same uniform render. What a semantic reviewer actually looks for is that adjacent sectioned parts do not share one lining, so the brief now requires exactly that relationship at each join, expressed as the strokes crossing the join line at different slopes, which is checkable in the pixels without dictating an angle.

The join line itself is kept, so even where hatching is read generously the base, each leg and the band remain bounded as separate bodies, which is what the description requires of a perimeter member standing proud of the second side and bearing on the covering element.

On FIG. 3 the earlier verified defect was a leader terminating on the crossing of the two cutting-plane lines. Moving the lines off the mid-lines removed the crossing from the centre, but the callouts still only said clear of both section lines. They now state the side of each line the dot must be on, which turns a negative clearance instruction into a positive region and leaves no candidate point on either line.

Both regions I named are the ones the lines leave open once the horizontal runs across the lower part and the vertical across the right-hand part, so the instructions are consistent with the line placement rather than in tension with it.

Hatch slope and line placement are sectioning conventions, so nothing about the invention moved. The four bodies, the flush legs at the perimeter of the underside, the legs resting on the band, the broken indicating line stopping at the base faces, the ring topology, both section designations with their arrows and both-end numerals, and every numeral target and list are unchanged.
The additions ran FIG. 3 long, so I compressed five phrases that repeated wording already present in the same brief.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged. Claim 1 rests on the rigid low-friction perimeter member at the perimeter of the second side, ending in a bearing face that leaves a clearance admitting ambient air continuously; an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric rate holds the chamber below atmospheric against that ingress; an all-rigid transmission path with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. FIG. 2 must keep showing the perimeter member as a separate rigid body hanging from the base and bearing on the covering element, since that is the structure separating the invention from the rubber-elastic apron of DE-202021002652-U1 and the elastic partitions of US-11408462-B2, and the join-line requirement secures that reading independently of hatch slope. Claims 10 and 20 remain dependent and keep the recital that the device advances while the differential is maintained, distinguishing US-4934475-A, whose vibration reduces the suction-adhering hold to permit travel, and US-10001245-B2, which floats on a blower-fed air cushion to move. US-11247858-B2 remains lifting and cleaning equipment that delivers no vibration into a laid covering element.

# FIG. 3 - Bottom plan view of the vibration device

**View:** Plan view looking straight up at the underside of the machine, nothing beneath the machine being drawn. Outline line work only; the only lettering drawn is the numeral 2 at both ends of one section line and the numeral 4 at both ends of the other.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet shows the underside of the machine as a rectangular ring in the manner of a picture frame. Two closed rectangular outlines appear, one within the other: the outer edge of the ring and the inner edge. The rectangular plan form is a convention for this sheet only, both parts shown schematically.

The perimeter member 24 is the ring surface. It runs continuously from the outer edge across to the inner edge as one plain surface, and all the way round, carrying round each corner without interruption, so that it reads as one closed loop. It is broad enough for a point well inside it to clear both edges.

The second side 16 is the face at which this view looks straight, appearing as the area held within the inner edge. That area is one plain face, bounded by the inner edge alone and continuous from that edge across to the opposite side, broad enough for a point well inside it to clear that edge.

Beyond the outer edge lies background. The ring stands well inside the drawing area, drawn large within it.

Two broken section lines cross the view, one horizontal across its lower part and one vertical across its right-hand part. Each begins and ends in the background just beyond the outer edge and crosses the ring surface and the face within it.

The horizontal line carries a short arrow at each of its two ends, both pointing toward the lower part of the sheet, and the numeral 2 at each of its two ends, so that it reads as section line 2-2 and leads to the sectional view of FIG. 2. The vertical line carries a short arrow at each of its two ends, both pointing toward the left-hand part of the sheet, and the numeral 4 at each of its two ends, so that it reads as section line 4-4 and leads to the sectional view of FIG. 4. It crosses the ring where the clearance is present.

The section lines are drawing conventions.

- The perimeter member 24 is the ring surface between the outer edge and the inner edge. Identified well inside that surface along the left-hand side of the ring, above the horizontal section line and clear of both section lines.
- The second side 16 is the plain face held within the inner edge. Identified well inside that face in its upper left region, above the horizontal section line and to the left of the vertical one, clear of both.

content.text: Both sheets are addressed and all six briefs are within the limit.

input.summary: Both sheets are repaired in their briefs. FIG. 2: the requirement that adjacent cut bodies carry hatching at different slopes is removed, since the renderer has produced one uniform lining through every formulation of it, and the separateness of the slab, each leg and the band now rests on the plain solid line drawn along each join, which the renderer does draw. The fluid-communication indication is also restated as two separate short broken lines rather than one line with a gap: the upper lies wholly within the housing and ends at the upper face of the base 12, the lower lies wholly within the chamber 22 and begins just below the lower face, and the hatched slab between them carries no broken line, so no passage through the base is asserted; the body count in the opening sentence now reads two broken lines to match. FIG. 3: the ring is now specified as exactly two closed rectangular outlines with the surface between them running unbroken from the outer edge straight to the inner edge along every side, so the view reads as a single frame of one width rather than two rings. Compressions keep FIG. 2 at 2791 and FIG. 3 at 2762 characters. No claim, numeral definition, description passage, drawing description or numeral list changed.
reasoning: The hatch-slope requirement has now failed on this sheet through five formulations: degrees, rising and falling, forward slash and backslash, stroke start and end points, and crossing at different slopes. It is a sectioning convention with no support in the sources, so continuing to demand it only guarantees a brief-to-pixel mismatch. Removing it and leaning on the join line keeps the three parts reading as three parts by a feature the renderer reliably produces.

The broken-line defect is different in kind and had to be fixed rather than relaxed, because a line running continuously through the base would depict the through-base passage that was expressly struck from this application. Describing two separate lines, each wholly inside a named region, replaces an instruction the renderer read as one interrupted line, and the sentence that the slab between them carries no broken line states the substantive point rather than an aesthetic one.
I corrected the opening enumeration to two broken lines so the brief counts what it now describes; a stale count is exactly the kind of internal mismatch a semantic review catches next.

On FIG. 3 the three-rectangle render is a recurrence of a defect that was cured once before by stating the topology positively, and the cure had since been diluted while the section lines were added. It is now stated twice over: exactly two closed outlines appear, and the surface between them runs unbroken from the outer edge straight to the inner edge along every side, so an intermediate outline would break a surface the brief requires to be continuous.
I described the frame as being of one width rather than banning a second boundary, keeping the instruction positive as required.

Both additions ran the briefs long, so I compressed phrases that repeated wording already present, including the arrow and designation sentences on FIG. 3 and two endpoint entries. # FIG. 3 - Bottom plan view of the vibration device

**View:** Plan view looking straight up at the underside of the machine, nothing beneath the machine being drawn. Outline line work only; the only lettering drawn is the numeral 2 at both ends of one section line and the numeral 4 at both ends of the other.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet shows the underside of the machine as one rectangular ring in the manner of a picture frame. Exactly two closed rectangular outlines appear, one within the other: the outer edge of the ring and the inner edge. The surface between those two outlines runs unbroken from the outer edge straight to the inner edge along every side, so the view reads as a single frame of one width. The rectangular plan form is a convention for this sheet only, both parts shown schematically.

The perimeter member 24 is the ring surface. It runs all the way round, carrying round each corner without interruption, so that it reads as one closed loop, and it is broad enough for a point well inside it to clear both edges.

The second side 16 is the face at which this view looks straight, appearing as the area held within the inner edge. That area is one plain face, bounded by the inner edge alone and continuous from that edge across to the opposite side, broad enough for a point well inside it to clear that edge.

Beyond the outer edge lies background. The ring stands well inside the drawing area, drawn large within it.

Two broken section lines cross the view, one horizontal across its lower part and one vertical across its right-hand part. Each begins and ends in the background just beyond the outer edge and crosses the ring surface and the face within it.

The horizontal line carries a short arrow at each end, both pointing toward the lower part of the sheet, and the numeral 2 at each end, so that it reads as section line 2-2 and leads to the sectional view of FIG. 2. It crosses the ring where the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element.

The vertical line carries a short arrow at each end, both pointing toward the left-hand part of the sheet, and the numeral 4 at each end, so that it reads as section line 4-4 and leads to the sectional view of FIG. 4. It crosses the ring where the clearance is present.

The section lines are drawing conventions.

- The perimeter member 24 is the ring surface between the two outlines. Identified well inside it along the left-hand side of the ring, above the horizontal section line.
- The second side 16 is the plain face within the inner edge. Identified well inside that face in its upper left region, above the horizontal section line and left of the vertical one.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 16, 24

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 16
- 24

reasoning: FIG. 3 has produced a third rectangle through several formulations that said how many outlines there should be. Stating a count leaves an extra line without a contradiction to violate, so the brief now enumerates the sheet's entire line work positively: two ring edges plus the two section lines and nothing else in the inventory. That is an inclusive description rather than a ban on a second boundary, and any extra outline is then a line the brief does not provide for.
I kept the continuity requirement as the second guard, since an intermediate outline would break a surface the brief requires to run unbroken from the outer edge to the inner edge along every side.

7	• Core apparatus - rigid base 12 with first side 14 and second side 16, vibration motor 18 on the first side, air-extraction mechanism 20 on the first side in fluid communication with chamber 22 on the second side, perimeter member 24 as a rigid loop/skirt at the perimeter of the second side: all from "providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt".
8	• Materials (claims 3, 13, 19; description) - "low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials".
9	• Non-seal / clearance 34 / continuous ingress (claims 1, 2, 11, 15) - "the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter". "Air entering beneath the rigid perimeter" supports the clearance along at least part of the member; the draft's "along at least part" hedge keeps it from overstating.

reasoning: The defect was substantive, not cosmetic. Two aligned broken stubs terminating exactly at the first side and resuming at the second side depict a route crossing the base at that place, which fixes both that a passage exists and where it enters and leaves. The sources give only the bare relationship, that the air-extraction mechanism is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side, and a through-base opening and duct were expressly struck from this application earlier.

The disclaimer that followed made it worse rather than better, since it told the sheet to show the two ends of a path and then told the reader no such path was asserted. That is the same instruct-then-deny pattern already removed from the FIG. 6 stirring-element paragraph, and a non-assertion cannot cure an affirmative geometry instruction.

Deleting the paragraph outright was the right remedy rather than rewording it, because any drawn indication of the route would carry the same implication. The relationship is a functional one the claims recite in words; it does not need to be drawn, and leaving it undrawn is the source-faithful choice given the disclosure supplies no route.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

input.summary: The preflight reported that the FIG. 6 brief's declaration was missing numeral 10 while the sheet list carried it, so the two are reconciled by declaring 10 again and giving it a target the sheet can actually deliver. Numeral 10 is now identified well inside the front face of the rectangular body, clear of the blocks and of the band, and the entry records that on this sheet the rectangular body stands for the whole machine and carries no other numeral, which is what keeps the assembly numeral from being read as a component label. The declaration line and the numerals list both read 10, 36 and 48, and the FIG. 6 entry in the Brief Description again names the vibration device among the parts shown schematically, so brief, sheet list and drawing description agree. The union of the six sheets still equals the seventeen-entry table. No claim, numeral definition, detailed-description passage or disclosed embodiment changed, and the brief is 2647 characters.
reasoning: The failure was an internal mismatch of my own making: I removed numeral 10 from the declaration last turn, but the sheet's machine-readable list still carried it, and the preflight compares the two before an image is generated. Reconciling them was the whole of the required repair.

I reconciled upward rather than downward, restoring the numeral, because the alternative leaves the sheet without any label for the device it depicts and depends on a re-render to rewrite the list, which is not something the brief can guarantee.

For the target I chose the body's broad front face rather than a boundary line. Three boundary formulations, including the one that passes on FIG. 1, produced a dot inside the face, and an interior region is the endpoint form this pipeline places reliably.

The earlier objection to an interior target was that the same drawn surface carries base numeral 12 on FIG. 1. I addressed that in the entry itself: on FIG. 6 the rectangular body stands for the whole machine and carries no other numeral, and neither the base nor the perimeter member is labelled on this sheet, so the leader cannot be read as identifying a component.

The Brief Description entry for FIG. 6 already named the vibration device among the parts shown schematically, which now matches the restored numeral, so no part is named as visible on a sheet whose list omits it and no further text change was needed.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile in perspective, as in FIG. 1, filling the lower part of the drawing area, its upper surface presented to the viewer as a broad open area. input.summary: The request is the standing gate instruction, so the work is the reported defect: numeral 36 on FIG. 6 was landing on the tile's front vertical face and bottom edge, with only a few units of clearance from visible lines. Both causes are addressed in the brief. The geometry now requires the open stretch of the tile's upper surface to the right of the machine to be drawn large and to run well back from the front edge of the tile, so a point can stand deep within it and far from every edge. The endpoint entry now names the surface expressly: numeral 36 is identified on the tile's upper surface, deep inside that open stretch to the right of the machine, well back from the front edge and well in from the right-hand edge, and not on any face below the upper surface. Compressions elsewhere in the same brief hold it at 2762 characters. Numerals 10 and 48 keep the targets settled in the previous rounds, the sheet still declares 10, 36 and 48 in both the declaration line and the list, and no claim, numeral definition, description passage, drawing description or numeral table entry changed.
reasoning: The three endpoint reviews agreed on the same thing: the dot was on the tile's front vertical face or its bottom edge rather than on the top surface the brief intended. In perspective the tile shows both a top surface and a front face, and the brief had been saying only open stretch of tile, which does not choose between them, so the fix had to name the upper surface and exclude the faces below it.

The separate grounding complaint, that the target had about seven units of clearance, is a size problem rather than a wording one, so I fixed the drawn area as well: the open stretch to the right of the machine is now required to be large and to run well back from the front edge, which is what gives an interior point room to sit far from every line.

# FIG. 6 - Third embodiment with stirring elements

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1. Outline line work only, with no lettering drawn. The vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism are omitted.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile in perspective, as in FIG. 1, filling the lower drawing area, its upper surface presented to the viewer as a broad open area. The machine stands on the left-hand part of that surface, and the open stretch to the right of the machine is drawn large, running well back from the front edge of the tile, so a point can stand deep within it and far from every edge.

The machine and the tile are shown schematically, the machine as one plain rectangular body standing on a band that runs round its underside, the band alone touching the tile, these forms being a convention for this sheet.

The band meets the underside of the body and follows the same run, its front surface facing the viewer as one unbroken strip across the whole width and drawn deep, its upper and lower edges well apart; its depth is schematic. It stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting the tile.

The rectangular body is drawn broad and tall, its front face turned toward the viewer as a large plain surface. The view being taken from the front left, the left-hand end of the body is also presented to the viewer, so that the body and the band together present one continuous outer boundary on that side.

Two small closed blocks, each a stirring element 48, are drawn carried by the machine on the front face of the rectangular body, each large enough that its own front face holds a point well inside it. They are shown schematically; their number, form and drawn position are a depiction convention for this sheet only, no engagement with the covering element 36 being asserted.

The whole drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine, the rectangular body with its band and the blocks it carries. Identified on the outer boundary line of the machine along the left-hand outer edge of the silhouette formed by the body and the band, clear of the front face of the body, of the blocks and of the band.
- The covering element 36 is that large plain tile. Identified on its upper surface, deep inside the open stretch of that surface to the right of the machine, well back from the front edge of the tile and well in from its right-hand edge, and not on any face below the upper surface.
- Each of the two small blocks is a stirring element 48. Identified well inside the front face of the left-hand block, clear of its edges.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 36, 48

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10
- 36
- 48

input.summary: Both findings are addressed in the figure briefs. FIG. 6's tile geometry is now the wording already proven on FIG. 1, one large plain tile in perspective filling the lower drawing area with the machine standing on its left-hand part and open tile to the right, and numeral 36 is identified well inside the open upper surface of the tile to the right of the machine, clear of every edge of the tile. That replaces the longer construction I had built around the tile's upper surface, which had produced an endpoint on the front face and a target region with almost no clearance. FIG. 3's numeral 16 no longer names a quadrant: it is identified well inside the face within the inner edge, clear of the inner edge and of both section lines, which is the broad interior form the endpoint guidance prefers and which matches an interior point anywhere on that face. The rendering of FIG. 6 as sheet 6 of 6 and the recording of its audit evidence are pipeline steps; figure files here are Markdown specifications and I created no image. FIG. 6 is at 2423 characters and FIG. 3 at 2751, and no claim, numeral definition, description passage, drawing description or numeral list changed.
reasoning: On FIG. 6 the instructive fact is that FIG. 1 carries the same tile with the same numeral and its endpoint passes. My successive attempts to specify the upper surface, the open stretch and the distances from each edge made the instruction longer without making it more placeable, and the last render put the dot on the front face. Adopting the wording that already works removes the divergence rather than adding another layer to it.

The endpoint entry keeps the one distinction that matters, that the point lies on the open upper surface of the tile rather than on a face below it, and otherwise states a broad interior target clear of every edge, which is the form the guidance calls for.

On FIG. 3 the quadrant instruction was the part adding nothing: the second side is a single plain face, so any interior point identifies it, and requiring an upper left region only creates a way for a correctly placed dot to be judged wrong. The replacement keeps the two clearances that do matter, from the inner edge and from both section lines, which is what prevents the leader from terminating on a cutting-plane line.
I did not touch numeral 24 on FIG. 3, which the evidence shows was traced successfully against its constraints, nor numerals 10 and 48 on FIG. 6, both settled in earlier rounds.

No application text was implicated by either finding. The Brief Description and the detailed description already describe FIG. 6 correctly, and the numeral table and sheet lists are unchanged, so the drawing set remains six sheets with the union of their numerals equal to the seventeen-entry table.

On the missing sheet itself I created no file. Figure files in this workspace are Markdown specifications and the images are generated from them, so the useful action available to me was to make the FIG. 6 brief render to a placeable target.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged. Claim 1 rests on the rigid low-friction perimeter member at the perimeter of the second side, ending in a bearing face that leaves a clearance admitting ambient air continuously; an air-extraction mechanism whose volumetric rate holds the chamber below atmospheric against that ingress; an all-rigid transmission path with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed; and a bearing face slidable while the differential is maintained. FIG. 3 shows that perimeter member as one closed loop around the second side and FIG. 6 shows the third embodiment, whose claims 10 and 20 keep the recital that the device advances while the differential is maintained, distinguishing US-4934475-A, where vibration reduces the suction-adhering hold to permit travel, and US-10001245-B2, which floats on a blower-fed air cushion to move. DE-202021002652-U1 and US-11408462-B2 remain distinguished by their compliant holding walls, and US-11247858-B2 by lifting and cleaning rather than delivering vibration into a laid covering element.
